api/index.html.title: API reference | DB Tools
api/index.html.summary: API reference This section is generated from the XML documentation comments in the source code. It lists the public types and members of the DB Tools assemblies. Generating the reference Run the documentation build from the repository root: bash .github/scripts/build-docs.sh full-api Use the SDK pinned by global.json. The script restores DocFX 2.78.5 from wiki/.config/dotnet-tools.json. It builds the Release product and Sandbox for Revit 2026 to supply build tasks, dependency assemblies and generated WPF source. The build runs on Linux with Windows targeting enabled. It does not start Revit. The script restores each non-test project in src/ with the metadata properties from wiki/docfx.json. DocFX's automatic restore is disabled because version 2.78.5 does not pass these properties to dotnet restore: Property Value Purpose Configuration Release Match the prerequisite builds and DocFX's default configuration. RevitYear 2026 Select the Revit API packages and year-specific restore assets. EnableWindowsTargeting true Resolve Windows and WPF reference packs on Linux. Set for every project by Directory.Build.props. DesignTimeBuild false Include Revit source excluded by XAML designer builds. DBT_IsDesignerBuild false Use normal project paths and source inclusion. _DBT_MergeDesigner true Retain public package references for DocFX's unmerged project symbols. _DBT_MergeDesigner controls package visibility separately from source inclusion. The product build merges public dependencies into their owning assemblies. DocFX reads project source, so its compilation needs those dependencies as package references. Keep the restore properties in the script aligned with the metadata properties in wiki/docfx.json. DocFX reads the projects in src/, excludes test projects, writes metadata to wiki/api/, and builds the site into wiki/_site/. Compilation errors fail the build. The conceptual script mode uses docfx-conceptual.json and builds the articles without API metadata or product builds. The reference covers the namespaces of DBTools.Core, DBTools.App, DBTools.Presentation and the tool assemblies (DBTools.GM, DBTools.SGT and others). Members without an XML comment appear without a description. Writing documentation comments Document each public type and member with /// comments. Give a <summary> for every member, a <param> for every parameter, <returns> for non-void methods and <exception> for exceptions that callers handle: /// <summary> /// Runs an action inside a Revit transaction. /// </summary> /// <param name="action">The action to run in the transaction.</param> /// <returns><see langword="true"/> if the transaction committed; otherwise <see langword="false"/>.</returns> /// <exception cref="InvalidOperationException">No document is active.</exception> public bool Execute(Action action) Use <remarks> only for constraints that a caller must know.

developer-guide/architecture/assembly-lo.title: Assembly Loading Contract | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/assembly-lo.summary: Assembly Loading Contract The product is a tree of ordinary files: one entry assembly, three top-level libraries and one assembly per tool. The installed add-in loads in Revit's default AssemblyLoadContext. Revit-hosted tests and Dev Mode load the product into a context that the dbtools-daemon creates. In every host, App loads each tool assembly by explicit path into the context that holds DBTools.dll, and Revit calls each command by its assembly path and class name. Installed layout Each supported year has one directory of ordinary files. This is the product tree that the installer, Revit-hosted test staging, Sandbox and Dev Mode use: <year>/ ├── DBTools.addin ├── DBTools.dll ├── DBTools.Core.dll ├── DBTools.Presentation.dll ├── DBTools.HandyControl.dll └── Tools/ ├── DBTools.AnalyticalSnapToLevel.dll ├── DBTools.DialogSuppression.dll ├── DBTools.ElevationTags.dll ├── DBTools.ERFT.dll ├── DBTools.FoundationTags.dll ├── DBTools.FramingJoins.dll ├── DBTools.GM.dll ├── DBTools.JoistGirderWeight.dll ├── DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes.dll ├── DBTools.RecordSet.dll ├── DBTools.SGT.dll ├── DBTools.Settings.dll ├── DBTools.TDV.dll └── DBTools.VTC.dll DBTools.addin names DBTools.dll and the class DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry. DBTools.dll contains the entry point and host infrastructure and no tool code. WPF needs the physical location of Presentation and HandyControl, so they stay at the top level. Merged libraries Every third-party runtime library is merged into one owner assembly; no third-party DLL is staged. build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props declares the merges: App owns ricaun.Revit.UI.0.9.0. Core owns the manifest and YAML parser, MVVM, functional, tessellation, dependency injection, logging, options and primitives libraries, and Serilog.Extensions.Logging. Presentation owns the Helix and SharpDX closure, Serilog, and the public dependency injection and logging abstractions. Serilog is in Presentation, which is never reloaded, because its thread-static state must not enter a collectible load context (dotnet/runtime#134928). A declaration's Include is the assembly name. The optional PackageId names a NuGet package whose name differs; ricaun uses PackageId="ricaun.Revit.UI" because its assembly name contains a version. MSBuild passes each merge its inputs as items: the resolved runtime asset of a package, or the output of a project. The merge copies its evaluated reference files into a temporary reference directory. ILRepack searches only that directory and resolves framework identities only from those files, so other package or compiler-output files and the runtimes installed on the build host cannot change the result. MSBuild Inputs and Outputs, including the owner's project.assets.json, decide when a merge reruns. The task deletes its temporary files afterwards. App host references The pinned ricaun.Revit.UI.0.9.0 assembly references Revit 27.0.4, also when App is compiled for Revit 2026. The App merge therefore binds these host references to the exact identities of the selected year during the final Cecil normalization: RevitAPI;RevitAPIUI;AdWindows;UIFramework Only App does this. MergeReferenceGuard then resolves every TypeRef, MemberRef and attribute type name with Cecil against the selected year's evaluated references. It rejects a missing type or member, a referenced version higher than the evaluated one, and any reference to an assembly that a merge removed. The Nice3point UIFramework reference is part of the Revit reference metadata used for this check; it is not shipped. Entry and idle acknowledgement AddinEntry has a public parameterless constructor for Revit. OnStartup first calls AddinIdle.TryAcknowledge. If DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set to any nonempty value and the entry assembly is in exactly AssemblyLoadContext.Default, it sets the AppContext data DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools to the entry assembly's file location and returns Succeeded before any runtime, ribbon, logging or tool work. OnShutdown returns Succeeded immediately for that instance. Otherwise startup enters AppStartupBoundary, a non-inlined method, which starts the App lifecycle inside ToolWindowCallbackScope. Startup, shutdown and ribbon failures that cannot reach the normal log are written to %APPDATA%\DBTools\Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log with BCL APIs only. Tool resolution ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly(rootAssembly, assemblyName) loads a manifest-declared assembly. The name must be a simple name without .dll or path characters. If it equals the root assembly's name, the root is returned. Otherwise the resolver: requires a file-backed root assembly; resolves <root directory>/Tools/<assemblyName>.dll and requires the file; reads the file's assembly name and requires the declared simple name; returns an assembly of that name already loaded in the root's context, if its full identity and location match the file; a different identity or location is an error; otherwise loads the file with that context's LoadFromAssemblyPath. The resolver does not search other contexts, install an AppDomain resolver or create a load context. The ribbon registers each command by its assembly location, full class name and availability type name. Availability is implemented by the command's own assembly. Command and availability callbacks enter ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the command's load context. Hosted tests and Dev Mode The daemon creates ProductLoadContext for hosted tests and DevModeLoadContext for Dev Mode. App loads each declared tool from Tools/ into that context; Dev Mode does not probe other subfolders. Presentation and HandyControl stay loaded for the life of the process. App, Core and the tool assemblies can be reloaded, as the host decides. Sandbox Sandbox runs one new process in the default context for each candidate year. Its entry point uses only BCL types: it validates the candidate, loads the top-level product files and the Tools/ assemblies from their paths, and then starts WPF through a non-inlined method. The process exits after validation, so no candidate assembly remains loaded for the next year. See Sandbox Validator. Distribution hashes Distribution validation checks the exact relative file set, PE identities, source-derived versions, first-party reference identities, file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. The hashes identify the staged candidate. Nothing checks them when an assembly loads. See Build Pipeline, Project References and Installation.

developer-guide/architecture/build-pipel.title: Build Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/build-pipel.summary: Build Pipeline build.sh (Linux, WSL) and build.ps1 (Windows, PowerShell 7) are the build entry points. Both run dotnet build build/Build.proj -t:<Target> with the pinned SDK; a plain dotnet build build/Build.proj -t:<Target> runs the same graph. The default target is BuildAll, which builds, validates and publishes the complete distribution for Revit 2026 and 2027. BuildAll compiles no test projects. Synopsis ./build.sh [Target] [parameters] pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 [Target] [parameters] Both entries print build/Usage.txt for --help. Option names ignore dashes and case. Option Short form Description --Configuration <Release\|Debug> -d, --debug Build configuration; -d selects Debug. Default: Release --Years <years> -y, --year Revit years, for example 2026 or "2026 2027". Default: every supported year --SkipClean <true\|false> --clean Skip Clean before Restore. --clean sets SkipClean to false. Default: true --Verbose [true\|false] -v, --verbose; -q, --quiet Show the child builds on the terminal; -q sets false. Default: false --DryRun [true\|false] Clean lists the directories and deletes none; BuildBundle writes no bundle; BuildInstaller prints the ISCC command instead of running it. The target's dependencies still run. Default: false --CandidateDistributionPath <dir> --candidate-dist Package an existing promoted tree --InnoSetupExe <path> Inno Setup compiler for BuildInstaller --Revit2026Dir <dir>, --Revit2027Dir <dir> Installed Revit, used only for validation --TestProjects <a,b> Projects for the selected-test targets An unknown option exits with status 2 before any SDK work, with Unknown build parameter '<option>'. The target is the first positional argument. build.sh rejects the NUKE options --target, --root, --solution, --continue, --nologo, --verbosity, --plan, --profile, --skip and --host with a message that starts ERROR: '<option>' is a NUKE option, and this build does not use NUKE. build.sh exits with status 3 in a Windows shell (Git Bash, Cygwin) and names build.ps1. Build.proj validates the option values in its Initialize step: a boolean other than true or false fails before any target runs. Targets Target Result BuildAll Complete 2026/2027 build, validation and promotion to .artifacts/dist/Release BuildApp [-y <year>] App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and the tool assemblies ValidatePrePush BuildApp plus manifest type validation BuildTests [-y <year>] Every test project and the hosted product inputs; all years by default BuildSelectedLocalTests, BuildSelectedPureTests, BuildSelectedDesignAutomationTests The projects named by --TestProjects in one test lane AssembleDistributionCandidate [-y <year>] A candidate year tree for checks that consume one; it is not published StagePortableAcceptanceInput Stage the candidate and Revit references for portable validation ValidateDistributionCandidate Portable validation and Dev Mode preflight of the candidate PackageSandboxValidationInput A content-addressed zip of the candidate and Sandbox for Windows validation PromoteToDist Replace the published distribution with the validated candidate BuildBundle Package the promoted tree into .artifacts/bundle/DBTools.bundle, one year tree per Revit year, under the Version.props product version BuildInstaller Build the bundle, then the installer with Inno Setup ValidateManifestTypes, VerifyArtifacts, BuildSandbox, BuildValidationRunner, Restore, Clean, Info Individual steps BuildAll, StagePortableAcceptanceInput, ValidateDistributionCandidate, PackageSandboxValidationInput, PromoteToDist, BuildBundle and BuildInstaller build the complete distribution. They require the Release configuration and the complete supported year set, which is the default; a -y that omits a supported year fails. ValidateDistributionCandidate and PromoteToDist also require a clean Git worktree. BuildBundle and BuildInstaller with --candidate-dist PATH package an existing promoted tree without building. --clean deletes build output; without it, an incremental BuildAll reuses the existing artifacts. No target switches to another SDK or output root. BuildAll depends on PromoteToDist, so it runs, in order: Restore, BuildValidationRunner (the Dev Mode policy runner), BuildApp for each year with ValidateProductVersions, VerifyArtifacts, StageDistributionCandidate, WriteCandidateMetadata, StagePortableAcceptanceInput, ValidateDistributionCandidate, ValidateManifestTypes and PromoteToDist. Examples ./build.sh BuildAll ./build.sh BuildAll --clean ./build.sh BuildApp --Configuration Debug --Years 2026 ./build.sh BuildTests ./build.sh BuildSelectedLocalTests --TestProjects DBTools.App.Local.Tests -y 2026 pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildAll Individual projects also build with plain dotnet build. Their MSBuild graph computes content versions and stages runtime prerequisites, but does not validate or publish a distribution. Implementation Each entry maps its options to MSBuild properties, acquires the pinned SDK, initializes the HandyControl submodule when needed, and runs Build.proj. Both entries produce the same dotnet build command line. No Build.proj target runs bash or Python, so BuildAll and BuildTests behave the same on Windows. Test execution is done by test.sh. Build.proj owns the target graph and starts each child dotnet build with its own binary log. The C# code of each target is a BuildPipelineStep in build/Tasks (DBTools.Build.Tasks, net8.0, loaded by the SDK's MSBuild on .NET 10). It owns option validation, Revit reference checks, Inno Setup discovery and the distribution steps. The task assembly is written to .artifacts/build-tasks/<Configuration>/ and recompiles only when its inputs change. Compilation on every operating system uses the centrally pinned Nice3point Revit API metadata packages with runtime assets excluded. An installed Revit is never a build prerequisite. --Revit2026Dir and --Revit2027Dir name an installation, native or mounted under WSL, for validation only. The staged Revit API files are reference metadata, not an executable runtime. APS Design Automation builds the separate Revit 2026 net8.0 Sentinel test project with its own API provider. Product output build/MSBuild/ProductOutput.proj and ProductOutput.targets stage the product tree for each year in .artifacts/bin/Release/<year>/net10.0-windows/. StageProductOutputTask keeps the Tools/ directory and validates each declared owner image. Intermediate runtime inputs can be year-keyed under .artifacts/bin/Release/<year>-runtime-input/. Local test staging copies the year tree recursively into the test output and removes stale top-level tool images. The installer receives the file list from DistributionContract.ProductFiles as the ISCC define ProductFiles and checks each year against it. Assembly merges build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props declares one owner for each merged library; AssemblyMerge.targets runs the merge. Every merged library is private to its owner and absent from the year tree, including Tools/. Each owner is merged once per build; MSBuild Inputs and Outputs skip the merge when nothing changed. The merger writes a deterministic MVID and PDB, and version validation requires each stable assembly (Presentation, HandyControl) to have the same version and SHA-256 in every year. Owner Merged libraries DBTools.dll (App) ricaun.Revit.UI DBTools.Core DBTools.Manifest, YamlDotNet, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm, CSharpFunctionalExtensions, LibTessDotNet, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, .Logging, .Options, .Primitives, Serilog.Extensions.Logging DBTools.Presentation HelixToolkit and SharpDX assemblies, Cyotek.Drawing.BitmapFont, CommunityToolkit.Diagnostics, Serilog, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions Serilog is in Presentation, which is never reloaded, because its thread-static state must not enter a collectible load context (dotnet/runtime#134928). The merge details are in Assembly Loading Contract. Content versions WPF resolves compiled resource URIs by assembly name and version, and Dev Mode identifies Presentation and HandyControl by full identity and SHA-256 hash. A content version therefore changes exactly when an assembly image can change. build/MSBuild/ContentVersion.targets computes it inside each ordinary compilation from these inputs: source, XAML and resource bytes, with the metadata that names, types and exposes each resource (Link, LogicalName, ManifestResourceName, Access, culture and generator metadata); resolved references: a package by its immutable coordinates, a project or local reference by its bytes, resolved before WPF markup compilation; source generators and the properties visible to them; the emitted assembly attributes, rendered as the SDK generates them, and the framework attribute; the signing key, Win32 manifest and resources, and the effective PathMap; the compiler options that change emitted code or metadata; for a merge owner, the merged project images and the merger code and binaries; for HandyControl, its vendor URI rewrite rules and the rewrite task's source (DBT_ContentVersionRule and DBT_ContentVersionInput). The content hash keys the rewrite, and a missing rewritten file reruns it. These are not inputs: build scripts and targets, .editorconfig and other analyzer configuration, diagnostic-only analyzers and warning options. Editing them changes no version. No Git commit or tree enters assembly attributes, content inputs or debug metadata. The computation runs inside the project's own compilation: it starts no second MSBuild evaluation and loads no other project. Because the inputs are hashed, resetting a source timestamp cannot hide changed bytes. A referenced content version is part of the referencing image, so consumers change version with it. An implementation-only change behind an unchanged version does not propagate through compiler references. The input list is written one entry per line to: .artifacts/obj/content-version/<Configuration>/<year|shared>-<flavor>/<project>/<framework>/inputs.txt The SHA-256 of the list is the input hash. Its first six bytes give the four-part assembly version: 4.<u16(bytes 0..1) % 65535>.<u16(bytes 2..3) % 65535>.<u16(bytes 4..5) % 65535> AssemblyInformationalVersion is <version>+inputs.<hash>. Compare two input lists to see why a version changed. Identical inputs keep the same identity and output timestamps. Content versions apply to Presentation, HandyControl, Core, App and projects that set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true. Other product metadata uses the release version from Version.props. Checked-in files are named relative to the repository root and artifacts relative to a relocatable root, so a fresh clone gives the same versions. Repository source and intermediate PDB documents use the path prefix /_/dbtools/; transformed vendor documents use /_/dbtools/vendor-build/. SourceLink revision stamping is off. A WPF temporary project hashes its parent's input list, so local-type identities in BAML carry the final version. The staged year trees carry the version evidence: each first-party image has its content version and input hash, the version must derive from that hash, and a stable image must be byte-identical in every year. The staging step reads them before it validates the compiled resource URIs. Candidate validation and promotion Distribution validation walks each year tree recursively. It requires the exact relative file set with Tools/ as the only directory, and checks PE identities, source-derived versions, first-party reference identities, framework references, and the length and SHA-256 of every file. It also checks the add-in entry, commands, availability types, manifests, resources and ownership. A missing, extra, misnamed, misplaced or stale file fails the candidate. Manifest validation scans every manifest.yml under src/ and resolves module, command, availability and design-time ViewModel type names against the compiled images of each year. Every declared owner must resolve to Tools/<owner>.dll. BuildAll and ValidatePrePush run it. ValidateDistributionCandidate prints one Dev Mode preflight line per year: Revit <year> Dev Mode preflight: <n> failures, <m> warnings; outcome=<x> Promotion requires a clean Git worktree (tracked and untracked files) with a resolved HEAD. Three records describe a distribution: The build metadata (build.json) records the years, frameworks, the distribution fingerprint, the Git commit and tree IDs, the source versions, the hash of each product file and the Protocol package pin. The portable acceptance receipt, written by ValidateDistributionCandidate, records for each year the validated files, the Revit reference descriptors and the Dev Mode preflight result. The promotion receipt, .artifacts/dist/Release/promotion-receipt.json, embeds the acceptance receipt with the source snapshot and the distribution fingerprint. It contains no temporary staging paths; consumers validate it against the published tree. Promotion validates the staged candidate, its fingerprint, the exact year trees and the receipt. It then deletes the published .artifacts/build.json, replaces .artifacts/dist/Release with the validated tree, copies the tool contract to .artifacts/acceptance/tool-contracts.json, and writes build.json last. Read the distribution only after the build command exits successfully. When promotion prepares the new tree, each declared file whose SHA-256 equals the file at the same path in the current .artifacts/dist/Release becomes a hard link to that file; new and changed files are copied. An unchanged file therefore stays the same file across promotions, and a virus scanner that has scanned it (Windows Defender on a Dev Mode host) does not scan it again. If the platform refuses a link (different file system, no hard-link support, permission error), promotion logs the reason once at low importance and copies that file and all remaining files. No step writes into a published file. Point Dev Mode at .artifacts/dist/Release/<year> directly; a copy is a set of new files that the scanner scans again. Tool contract build/Distribution/tool-contracts.json holds the DBTools texts that the live Tools check of dbtools-daemon compares with the running product: window titles, interaction kinds, prerequisite refusal names, and banner, control and status texts. Its tools object is keyed by command type name without the Command suffix (Gm for GmCommand). Each entry has interaction, title (null for a command without a window), source_files and named texts. PromoteToDist publishes it as .artifacts/acceptance/tool-contracts.json, so a distribution archive carries it beside build.json: the CI dbtools-complete artifact and the release assets include it. Clean keeps .artifacts/acceptance/. Change a source text that an entry names and this file in the same commit. ToolContractsTests in testing/DBTools.Build.Tests fails when a source_files path does not exist, or when a text equals no whole string value of its tool's source files: ./test.sh test --tool BUILD --fixture ToolContractsTests The string values are C# string literals, XAML attribute values and text with XML references resolved, and YAML scalar values; a longer string such as General Settings does not match General. Three forms also match: each line of a multi-line C# literal, because a refusal message reaches the log one line at a time; a ribbon displayText with its lines joined by spaces, which is the command's execution name; and a C# interpolated string or a XAML StringFormat whose holes each take a whole string value from the same files. Two values are not product text. Gm.workspace_status_pattern is a regular expression that the check applies to the GM status text; the test requires that it compiles. The check fails a refusal log that contains UpdateCombinedFoundationTags.invalid_message; the test requires that no string of the tool's source files contains it. Revit-hosted test inputs Staging for Revit-hosted tests builds one complete product tree for the selected year and includes it with relative paths unchanged, including the 14 tool assemblies in Tools/. Test assemblies, NUnit and adapter files, and companions are separate inputs. The input cache checks relative path, identity, length and hash before the daemon request is written. Test restore roots are per year: each year of the local scope restores separately, and Design Automation tests share the 2026 root. The Pure root restores every Pure project against $(DBT_PureRevitYear) owners through static graph restore. NuGet keys package specifications by project path, so one root never mixes owner variants. See Test Pipeline. Pinned SDK build/DotNet/sdk.sh selects the SDK version from global.json. If no installed dotnet has that SDK, it uses the private root ~/.dotnet/pinned-sdk-<version>. A system dotnet with the pinned SDK is used as is. A build needs only the SDK. A net8.0 test host (the APS Design Automation Sentinel) also needs the .NET 8 runtime. sdk.sh pins that runtime version, because global.json cannot, and installs it only when such a host runs: test.sh requests it, or run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. On a system dotnet without the .NET 8 runtime, a net8.0 test host uses the private root. A package in the private root is valid only when its marker file, .dbt-complete-<package>-<version>, names its archive. To install a package, sdk.sh: checks the archive against the SHA-512 in Microsoft's release metadata; extracts it into a staging directory beside the root; renames the version directories into place; writes the marker. A version directory without a valid marker is replaced from the verified archive; one that already matches stays. The lock <root>.lock serializes installs across builds and worktrees, and a build that waited for the lock checks the markers again before it installs anything. The Linux installer requires Python 3.10 or later. build.ps1 uses the same root, SHA-512 check, marker and lock for the SDK without Python. It downloads the release metadata's dotnet-sdk-win-<arch>.zip and replaces a root without a valid marker as a whole. It installs no test-host runtime. Build servers DBT_BUILD_SERVERS sets the server mode for every wrapper invocation (build.sh, test.sh, the lane helpers and their child builds). DBT_MSBUILD_MAX_CPU_COUNT sets the graph build parallelism (default 2); the wrappers validate it and Build.proj passes it to its child builds. build.sh runs Build.proj itself without the MSBuild server; each child dotnet build uses the selected mode. 1 (default): the invocation owns one compiler server and one MSBuild server. Its scope ID, dbtools-scope-<owner pid>-<run id>, is the compiler pipe name, and <scope id>-msbuild is the MSBuild handshake salt. On every trapped exit, each server gets a shutdown request with a 30 s timeout; then every process the invocation still owns is terminated, the compiler by its exact -pipename: argument and MSBuild nodes by the exact salt in their environment. No process is matched by name. A starting invocation stops dbtools-scope servers whose owner process no longer exists; servers of a live owner are never touched. The servers make a clean build faster and raise its peak memory use. 0: no compiler server and no MSBuild server (UseSharedCompilation=false). Use this on hosts that admit builds by free memory. build.ps1 always uses mode 0, because the ownership checks read Linux /proc. Node reuse is off in both modes. Outside a wrapper, Directory.Build.props keeps the compiler server off. UseSharedCompilation is not a content-version input. build/Testing/check-build-server-lifecycle.sh <second-checkout> runs the server lifecycle with the real SDK: a normal exit, a failed build, SIGTERM, SIGKILL followed by the next build's sweep, and a concurrent owner in another checkout. Run it manually. Logs Each run writes to .artifacts/build/<YYYYMMDD-HHmmssfff>-<pid>/, named by build.sh or build.ps1 (by Build.proj for a plain dotnet build). The folder holds the full plain-text console.log at detailed verbosity and one binary log per child build. When the build ends, successfully or not, the entry writes a completed marker and copies the log to .artifacts/build/console.log. Each run first prunes old folders. It keeps the ten newest completed folders, deletes folders that contain only a marker, deletes unmarked folders after 24 hours without activity, and skips folders whose process is still running. Test builds write .artifacts/build/test-matrix.binlog, replacing the previous one. The terminal shows per-step progress, errors, warnings, the Dev Mode preflight lines and the MSBuild summary. --verbose adds the child build output. The file log is always detailed. Directory layout Path Contents .artifacts/bin/<Configuration>/<Year>/<TFM>/ Compiler output; the shared bucket when no year is selected .artifacts/obj/ Intermediate output and content-version input lists .artifacts/vendor/<Configuration>/handycontrol/net10.0-windows/ HandyControl build output .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ Sandbox build output .artifacts/.staging/<build id>/distribution-candidate/Release/ Candidate distribution .artifacts/dist/Release/<year>/ Published distribution, with promotion-receipt.json in .artifacts/dist/Release/ .artifacts/build.json Build metadata of the published distribution .artifacts/acceptance/tool-contracts.json Tool contract of the published distribution .artifacts/bundle/, .artifacts/installer/ Bundle and installer .artifacts/build/ Run logs Directory.Build.props defines the output and object roots. WPF temporary projects (_wpftmp) get a separate intermediate path. The standard target framework is net10.0-windows; Design Automation uses net8.0-windows. Directory.Build.targets adds host warnings, project-reference routing, WPF designer fixes and product and test staging hooks. HandyControl HandyControl is built from the vendor/HandyControl submodule through build/HandyControl/DBTools.HandyControl.csproj. The project imports the four upstream shared .projitems files and the upstream resources, writes transformed intermediate copies that use the DBTools assembly name and versioned pack URIs, and compiles Shared/Themes/Theme.xaml as the theme. The upstream project-root Theme.xaml generated by its PreBuild step is not an input. A missing submodule, resource or transform input fails with its path. Concurrency Run one build or test command per worktree at a time. Concurrent builds need separate BaseArtifactsDir roots; sharing compiler or WPF output between roots is not supported. A nested test command reuses the build-server scope of its parent. build.sh, build.ps1 and test.sh take no lock and do not check free memory. Continuous integration The CI and Documentation workflows run only on manual dispatch, not on pushes or pull requests. CI mode build runs BuildAll; mode build-test also builds and runs the selected tests. The Documentation workflow publishes the site through the wiki server. The release workflow, triggered by a published release, builds and promotes the distribution and bundle on Linux, then runs only the Inno Setup compiler on Windows. The self-hosted Windows test runner consumes compiled test artifacts through test.sh and does not build the product. The Claude Code workflow accepts created issue comments and pull request review comments that mention @claude. Bot comments are excluded. The case-insensitive @claude[[:space:]]*review test selects reviews within a line. A review request on a plain issue fails. Other admitted requests use the general job with its write and OIDC permissions. Both model jobs use CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and claude-opus-4-7. For reviews, classification checks out the repository default branch. It reads the pull request API, fetches the numeric pull ref and base commit with full history, checks the head SHA, and prepares the merge-base-to-head diff. The numeric pull ref supports fork branches. No pull request scripts or Git hooks run. The review job has repository and pull request read permissions. It checks the source SHA again and reads the prepared diff and context. Claude runs in native plan mode with only Read, Grep, and Glob. Restricted mode confines file tools to the workspace and prepared-data directory. Read rules deny Git metadata. MCP tools and ordinary customizations are disabled. Local managed policy files prevent review because safe mode and ordinary disableAllHooks settings cannot disable managed hooks. The review and general jobs stop after 60 minutes. Validation requires a successful action, one successful terminal SDK result, the requested init and assistant model identities, usage for that model, native plan mode, the three approved tools, and nonempty final text. Helper models in usage accounting are permitted. Text containing either job credential, known Base64 credential forms, or common token patterns fails validation. Only validated final text crosses to publication in a JSON artifact named for the current run and attempt. Execution logs and token outputs do not cross that boundary. Publication has only pull request write permission, no provider credential, and no source checkout. Issue-comment requests receive one PR conversation comment. Review-comment requests receive one reply in the original review thread. The classified event determines the destination. Returned text remains literal data. Publication errors fail the job. ClaudeCodeWorkflowTests.WorkflowSecuritySuitePasses runs the workflow's inline scripts with event, API, and SDK fixtures. It requires Python 3, PyYAML, Node.js, and grep. It does not invoke GitHub Actions or authenticate to the provider: ./test.sh test --tool BUILD --scope pure --fixture ClaudeCodeWorkflowTests Source maps and CANON These checks are run by the pre-push hook and CI, not by any build target: python3 .agents/work/canon_source_maps.py writes one MAP.md beside each manifest. A map lists the current source tree, including untracked files that are not ignored, and labels test folders as test mirrors. --check recomputes the maps byte for byte (UTF-8, LF) and fails if one is stale. python3 .agents/work/canon_source_fidelity.py --gate checks folder and namespace agreement, type and file identity, repeated declarations, vocabulary and unresolved rulings for the declared source roots. Troubleshooting Problem Action dotnet or the pinned SDK is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh. The .NET 8 runtime for the Design Automation Sentinel is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. HandyControl output is missing Run the build from a Git checkout with network access, so the entry can initialize the submodule. WPF designer output collides Build through the repository targets, so _wpftmp gets its own intermediate path. MSBuild task DLLs stay locked A wrapper killed past its exit trap leaves its servers running until the next wrapper invocation stops them. Run the command again. A focused build is slow Build the project or use BuildApp; keep BuildAll for the full distribution. See Project References, Test Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.title: Architecture Overview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.summary: Architecture Overview DB Tools is a suite of Revit add-in tools. Revit loads one entry assembly, DBTools.dll, built from src/DBTools.App. App loads shared infrastructure from DBTools.Core.dll, stable WPF types from DBTools.Presentation.dll, and each tool from its own assembly in the Tools/ directory. flowchart TB Revit[Revit Host] -->|DBTools.addin| App[DBTools.dll / App] App --> Core[DBTools.Core.dll] App --> Presentation[DBTools.Presentation.dll] Presentation --> Handy[DBTools.HandyControl.dll] App -->|explicit path: Tools/| Tools[Tool assemblies] Core --> RevitAPI[Revit API] Components Project Assembly Responsibility src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Revit entry point, startup and shutdown, service composition, ribbon, embedded tool manifests src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Shared execution (call gate, transactions, safe execution), settings, logging, tool registry, manifest loading, tool assembly resolution src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll WPF resources, themes, controls and window shells that live for the whole Revit process build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed build of the vendored HandyControl library src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> DBTools.<Tool>.dll One tool: its module, commands, features and views src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Candidate validator and UI development host that runs without Revit Presentation references only WPF and HandyControl. App, Core and the tools may reference Presentation. See Project References. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, not into Application.Resources, so DB Tools does not change other add-ins. See Theme System. Product tree Each supported Revit year has one directory with DBTools.addin, the four top-level assemblies and the 14 tool assemblies in Tools/; see Installed layout. The build merges every third-party runtime library into one owner assembly, so the directory contains no other DLLs. The installer, Revit-hosted test staging, Sandbox and Dev Mode use the same tree. See Build Pipeline. Load contexts The installed add-in runs in Revit's default AssemblyLoadContext. For Revit-hosted tests and Dev Mode, the dbtools-daemon loads the product into its own context (ProductLoadContext or DevModeLoadContext). DB Tools creates no load context of its own. App loads each tool assembly into the context that already holds DBTools.dll. Startup DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry implements IExternalApplication. OnStartup runs these steps in order: Idle check. If DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set and the entry assembly is in the default load context, the add-in sets the AppContext key DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools to the entry assembly's location and returns Succeeded without further work. OnShutdown then also returns immediately. This lets the daemon run a Revit that has the installed add-in while it tests its own copy. Callback scope. AppStartupBoundary (not inlined) enters ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the entry assembly's load context. Runtime. App reads the Revit year from VersionNumber, creates the logging host and the service provider, and publishes them through AppRuntimeAccessor. Theme validation. ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow loads and freezes the theme dictionaries and lays out a probe control tree. Ribbon. App composes the ribbon from the embedded manifests. Background startup. App starts the local Revit task host and an asynchronous startup task that installs the Revit main-window owner provider and attaches tool hooks. Publication. App registers an Idling handler for failed-startup cleanup, then the deferred startup handlers (ApplicationInitialized and Idling), and publishes the started state. A failure in steps 3 to 6 cleans up what was created and returns Failed. A failure of the background task is cleaned up on the next Idling event. Failures that cannot reach the normal log are written to %APPDATA%\DBTools\Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log with BCL APIs only, so this log works before Core loads. Tools and commands Each tool has a manifest.yml that names its assembly, module type, commands and availability types. App embeds all manifests. At startup: ToolModuleCatalog loads and validates the embedded manifests once. The App registrar loads each declared assembly with ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly, which loads only <entry directory>/Tools/<name>.dll. The registrar creates each module, collects its settings, services, settings packs and hooks, checks ownership, and merges them into the App service collection. Manifests without a module register only ribbon items. ToolRegistry.MergeFrom validates every incoming tool and hook against the existing registrations before it changes anything, so a conflict leaves the registry unchanged. Duplicate internal names are rejected. The ribbon refers to each command by its assembly location and full type name. When a command runs, CommandPreflight checks, before any run scope exists, that its ribbon panel is enabled in Settings, that its availability type allows it, and that no active feature warning disables it. Only then does CommandContextFactory create the run scope with the command's execution profile. Settings-only and hook-only tools still have a manifest and a module. Services and scopes The App service provider holds application-lifetime services: logging, settings, hooks, ISafeExecutor, the tool registry and ribbon state. Each command run, modeless session or test opens a scope that holds the Revit run scope (IRevitRunScope), its IRevitCallGate, ITransactionRunner and ITransactionGroupService. Command, availability and window callbacks enter ToolWindowCallbackScope. Source layout Tool source is under src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/ with namespace root DBTools.<Tool>. Folders are named for what they own, for example App/, Features/, Domain/, Revit/, Settings/, Assets/ and Tests/. A tool has only the folders it needs. Generic folders such as Helpers, Models or Infrastructure are not used for production code. Supported years Desktop Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027 both target net10.0-windows. build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs defines the supported years. APS Design Automation tests use a separate Revit 2026 net8.0-windows profile. Build and validation build.sh (Linux, WSL) and build.ps1 (Windows) run build/Build.proj. BuildAll builds, validates and publishes the complete two-year distribution. BuildApp, BuildTests and test.sh build smaller graphs. See Build Pipeline and Test Pipeline. Distribution validation records the length and SHA-256 of every file in the candidate. These hashes identify what was built and tested. They do not authenticate assemblies at load time.

developer-guide/architecture/project-ref.title: Project References | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/project-ref.summary: Project References Desktop Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027 use one target framework, net10.0-windows. build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs and build/MSBuild/RevitTargetFrameworks.props define the supported years and their framework. Projects use $(DBT_RevitTargetFramework) and contain no year-specific framework conditions. Assemblies Project Assembly Role src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Revit entry point, App lifecycle and host infrastructure, embedded tool manifests src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Shared execution, settings, logging, tool registry, manifest loading, tool assembly resolution src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll Stable WPF resources, controls and window shells build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll Renamed HandyControl build src/DBTools.Manifest merged into Core Portable manifest.yml parser (net8.0) for build tooling and validation src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> DBTools.<Tool>.dll One tool: commands, features and tool services src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Candidate validation and UI development without Revit Reference direction App references Core and Presentation. It embeds every src/Tools/**/manifest.yml as a resource and compiles no tool source. Core references Presentation and DBTools.Manifest. It references the Revit API where a shared capability needs it. Tools reference Core, and Presentation for their UI. Presentation references only WPF and HandyControl. It does not reference App, Core, tool types or the Revit API. Sandbox compiles against Core, Presentation and HandyControl without copying their runtime files, and loads them from the candidate year directory at run time. App owns the ricaun.Revit.UI compile reference; the merge folds its runtime into DBTools.dll. Add a third-party runtime dependency through a declared merge in build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props, not through a copy step. See Assembly Loading Contract. Tool assemblies Set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true in a project that produces a shipped tool assembly. The build stages its output in the year's Tools/ directory and gives it a content-derived version. At run time App resolves the tool through ToolAssemblyResolver, which loads into the context of the App and Core root assembly. The same rule applies in the default context, in the daemon's ProductLoadContext and in DevModeLoadContext. Every manifest under src/Tools/ has its own assembly, including Settings, the Super Girt Tool (SGT) and DialogSuppression. A tool assembly must not contain a copy of Core or of Presentation. Test references Pure projects use the ordinary compile and runtime graph of their scope. Revit-hosted (.Local.Tests) projects receive the selected year's host references and the staged product tree with Tools/ intact. Input generation for Revit-hosted tests keeps the product root separate from test assemblies and adapter dependencies. A project reference must not place product assemblies flat beside a test assembly: the product requires the year root and its Tools/ subdirectory. Keep a dependency's host or resource constraint in the project that owns it, and validate the resulting candidate tree. Do not add projects for unsupported frameworks or a second load context for DB Tools. See Assembly Loading Contract, Build Pipeline and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.title: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.summary: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay DB Tools runs all Revit API work through a call gate, inside a run scope that each command, modeless session or test owns. Tool windows report long operations through the progress overlay. This page owns the design of run scopes, call gates, transaction services and the progress overlay. DBTools.Core describes the rest of the Core library and its source folders. Command entry ToolCommand (src/DBTools.Core/Tools/Commands/ToolCommand.cs) is the base class of every Revit command. Its public Execute runs the command body inside ISafeExecutor and gives the protected RunAsync hook one owning CommandContext; see ToolCommand for the API. Command subclasses resolve services from ICommandContext. Its base interface IAppRunScope exposes the scope's RevitRunScope and Resolve<T>(). A feature that owns a window composes ToolWindowFactory and calls IToolWindowSession.ShowDialog() or Show(). The session owns the reflection scope and the window's retirement. An expected refusal throws SafeExecutionRefusedException with a reason for the user. SafeExecutor then returns SafeExecutionStatus.Refused, with no failure surface and no exception diagnostics. SafeExecutionRefusalReporter shows a Warning banner, which writes the one Warning log entry; an execution without a banner logs [Refused] {Name}: {Message}. ToolCommand returns Revit Result.Cancelled for a refusal and for a failure. An unexpected exception writes Error diagnostics and shows an Error banner. Run scopes App composition (AppServiceProviderFactory) registers IAppRunScopeFactory with the Core implementation AppRunScopeFactory. CommandContextFactory calls Create(UIApplication, AppRunScopeProfile). The factory selects the call gate for the profile, constructs RevitRunScope, and returns the concrete AppRunScope, which owns scoped service resolution, its IRevitRunScope and disposal. Construction and disposal keep the primary failure, attempt every owned cleanup step and report further cleanup failures in order. Profile Call gate Use InlineUi (default) InlineRevitCallGate Modal commands and daemon-hosted Revit automation that already run on the Revit UI thread. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless tool windows and long workflows that must queue Revit API work to the UI thread through the App-owned ExternalEvent host. A tool selects its profile through RunProfile in its manifest; ToolRegistration uses InlineUi when none is given. IRevitRunScope owns the UIApplication, the call gate, document access and disposal. Transaction services are scoped registrations, resolved with Resolve<T>() on IAppRunScope or ICommandContext. public interface IRevitRunScope : IDisposable { UIApplication UIApplication { get; } IRevitCallGate CallGate { get; } UIDocument GetActiveUiDocument(); Document GetActiveDocument(); Document GetVerifiedActiveDocument(Document expectedDocument, string? context = null); } A consumer that keeps its launch document calls GetVerifiedActiveDocument(...). The run scope rejects an invalid expected or active document and requires matching DocumentSessionKey values before it returns the active document. RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers only the Revit-scoped run-scope access, the call gate and the transaction services. The App composition root registers IAppRunScopeFactory, safe execution, command preflight and the command context services. Call gates IRevitCallGate is the single entry point for Revit API access. It runs synchronous callbacks on the Revit UI thread. Revit API calls outside the call gate can raise invalid-context exceptions or break UI-thread rules. public interface IRevitCallGate { bool InGate { get; } Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); } Mode Behavior Auto Run inline when the caller already has a gate context; otherwise queue through the owned ExternalEvent host. ForceQueue Always queue through the owned ExternalEvent, in a later turn. The inline gate rejects it with ContextUnavailableException. InlineRevitCallGate(UIApplication) runs delegates immediately on the Revit UI thread with the supplied application. Modal commands use it. QueuedRevitCallGate schedules the callback through its ExternalEvent host. QueuedRevitCallGate and the host's RevitCallGateTask each require an ILogger from their composition owner; App passes its runtime logger to AppLocalRevitTaskLifecycle.Start. A missing logger is a construction error. The active UIApplication, the queued-gate depth and the Revit-test depth are internal scoped state. QueuedRevitCallGate owns the queued and test scopes; RevitRunScope owns its application context token. Every scope restores the exact previous value, and a repeated disposal does nothing. Delegate admission Admission is synchronous and runs before the gate validates the API context or schedules anything. Keep asynchronous workflows outside the gate and make in-gate delegates synchronous: await _gate.RunAsync(app => { // Revit API work here (synchronous only) return true; }); Every member of an Action invocation list is checked for an async state machine, so an async void action is rejected. A delegate whose result type is Task, Task<T>, ValueTask or ValueTask<T>, including nullable ValueTask, is rejected. A multicast result delegate with a reference result type is rejected, because ordinary multicast dispatch exposes only the last return value. After invocation, a reference-typed result gets a runtime Task/ValueTask check, which also finds interface-typed Task and boxed ValueTask values. Custom awaiter structs are not detected. Sources: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/{CallGateDelegateValidator,InlineRevitCallGate,QueuedRevitCallGate,RevitCallGateTask,RevitCallGateTaskQueue}.cs. API-context admission RevitCallGateApiContext.IsActive decides whether the current code has Revit API context. Known native entry points use the internal synchronous Enter scope. An untracked call first checks the Revit dispatcher thread, then creates and immediately disposes an unraised ExternalEvent with a stateless no-op handler. Worker threads return false before the probe. Every untracked call probes again. No result is cached across turns. Current exposes a known UIApplication only while the context is active. An ambient application reference does not grant API context. The public UIApplication constructor requires ApplicationServices.Application; there is no public conversion from UIControlledApplication.ControlledApplication. If startup has not received a UIApplication, queued work gets one from the real ExternalEvent callback. No private-field reflection is used. The probe creates a new event instead of adding and removing a handler on a Revit event. It does not change the subscriber collection of the current event and does not write a document, so it is legal in Idling, ViewActivated, DocumentChanged and updater callbacks. Admission does not permit an API that a particular callback forbids; callers must obey read-only and dynamic-update restrictions. The 2026 and 2027 API references list the Create signature and the null-handler exception, but not the outside-context exception. An Autodesk forum thread describes that runtime check and the difference between UI-thread access and API context. The probe does not identify which add-in owns a callback. Inside another add-in's main-thread API callback it returns true, and DB Tools runs inline without its own scope. Callbacks that DB Tools owns enter an explicit synchronous UIApplication scope; later continuations must probe or queue again. The scope is a ref struct, so a caller cannot hold it across an await. Its shared lifetime lets a wrong-thread disposal revoke the context before the misuse is reported. Enter is internal; App's native callbacks and FoundationTags' Idling owner use it. Global Mapper (GM) has access for synchronous-delegate validation only and does not enter scopes. Queued turns Each native Execute turn of the queued gate runs, in FIFO order, every item that was waiting when the turn started. N waiting calls cost one Revit round trip. Items queued during a turn wait for the next turn. After the first item, a turn starts no new item once its 50 ms budget (RevitCallGateTask.DrainBudget) is used. A failed or canceled item completes its own task; the turn continues with the next item. An item that leaves a transaction open in any document ends the turn. Revit discards what a callback leaves open only when the callback returns, so the next item must run in a later turn. An item that creates a transaction group through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin also ends the turn. Nested Auto calls run inline. ForceQueue defers to a later turn. A caller that needs several reads for one user action makes them in one RunAsync body, or starts independent calls together so that one turn runs them all. A transaction group without an open transaction is not visible to the open-transaction check. Production code therefore creates every TransactionGroup through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin(document, name, validateStart). The factory calls RevitCallGateTurnBoundary.EndAfterCurrentCall(), so the current turn ends when the running call returns, then constructs and starts the group and disposes it if the start fails. The build contract suite (TransactionGroupTurnBoundaryContractTests) inspects the compiled production assemblies and rejects TransactionGroup construction outside that factory. The scheduler posts every raise to the Revit dispatcher at Normal priority, also from the dispatcher thread. A caller never waits on native Raise, a burst of calls shares one raise, and the raise for work left after a turn runs after Execute returns. Denied and TimedOut raise results keep the queue and retry with a backoff from 50 ms, doubling to at most 500 ms, for at most 5 seconds (RevitCallGateRaiseRetry). When that time expires, the waiting batch faults; the scheduler still accepts new work. Each turn feeds a Debug summary with the prefix [CallGate/Turns]: turns and calls, maximum queue depth, the Raise-to-Execute gap, Execute duration, native Raise duration and results, and refused-raise retries. The summary is written when a turn leaves the queue empty, at most once per second, or after 10 s of a queue that stays busy. Turns inside the one-second interval are reported with the next activity. Retirement cancels the posted raise, stops and detaches the retry timer, releases queued delegates and disposes the native event. Dropped tasks never complete, so a worker that waits synchronously on one hangs. Cleanup after a failed startup cancels the tasks instead, because Revit and its callers are still running. Transactions Resolve transaction services from the command scope: context.Resolve<ITransactionRunner>() and context.Resolve<ITransactionGroupService>(). RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers both as scoped services on the scope's IRevitCallGate. ITransactionRunner public interface ITransactionRunner { Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); } Delegates receive RevitTransactionContext, which carries the UIApplication and the Document. TransactionRunner runs on IRevitCallGate and applies the synchronous delegate admission before it enters the gate or starts a transaction. The runtime awaitable check for a reference-typed result runs inside the transaction body, so an awaitable result rolls the transaction back before commit. If doc.IsModifiable (a transaction is already open), it uses a SubTransaction; otherwise it starts a Transaction. It refuses to start a transaction on one document while another document is modifiable. It attaches TransactionFailurePreprocessor, which suppresses non-critical Revit warnings. await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => { Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false); }); var wallId = await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false).Id); Failure handling TransactionRunner collects failures through transaction or subtransaction disposal before returning a result. The first operation failure stops further work. Existing work/rollback aggregates precede any disposal failure. A single failure keeps its identity, type and original stack. Multiple failures propagate in an ordered aggregate. A disposal failure after commit propagates without undoing the committed write. TransactionFailurePreprocessor.AttachToTransaction sets clear-after-rollback before failure processing starts. A warning is reported as suppressed only after Revit deletes it. A blocking failure, or a fault in a failure accessor, records a blocking diagnostic and requests rollback. An accessor fault keeps the caught exception, which becomes the InnerException of the TransactionFailureException (an AggregateException when several accessors failed). An attachment fault propagates before commit; the preprocessor does not change rollback options inside the failure callback. The preprocessor keeps one TransactionFailureRecord per message it reads: severity, description, failure definition GUID, failing element IDs and whether the message rolled the transaction back. A fault while reading the failing element IDs is added to AccessorFaults and does not change how the message resolves. A runner built with new TransactionRunner(gate, logger) logs every record and every accessor fault at Warning after the commit; the one-argument constructor logs nothing. GM's apply runners use the logging form. TransactionFailureException is the public diagnostic for a transaction that did not reach Committed. Its constructors are internal to Core. Callers read the transaction name, final status, warnings, blocking failure text and failure-definition identities from its properties. A posted blocking failure rolls back a runner-managed transaction and raises this exception with the transaction name and the blocking diagnostic. Tool write boundaries map this exception and Revit refusal exceptions to their own typed failures and keep the original exception as the inner cause. Sources: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Transactions/{TransactionRunner,TransactionExecutor,TransactionBoundary,TransactionFailurePreprocessor}.cs. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService makes several transactions on the active document one Revit undo entry. It is the manual lifecycle; the caller owns the try/finally around FinalizeAsync, in the workflow that knows whether to commit or roll back. public interface ITransactionGroupService { bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); } If the document is already modifiable, BeginAsync creates no group, IsActive becomes true, and FinalizeAsync only resets state. FinalizeAsync accepts only TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit (assimilate) and Rollback; another value fails before the inactive-session check. Finalization always clears the active group state and attempts disposal of the owned group. If the operation and the cleanup both fail, the operation failure comes first in an ordered aggregate. Revit rolls back a group that is still open when the API callback that started it returns, and RevitTransactionGroups.Begin ends the queued turn after the current call. Separate BeginAsync and FinalizeAsync calls therefore keep one group only on an InlineUi gate inside one callback, as the modal Super Girt Tool (SGT) and Transfer Drafting Views (TDV) commands use them. Queued modeless work uses IAtomicTransactionGroup.RunAsync(name, work, keep, ct), which TransactionGroupService also implements; GM commit review constructs it directly for its gate. In one gate call it begins the group, runs the work, then assimilates the group when keep(result) is true and rolls it back otherwise. The group is one Revit undo entry also under the queued gate. An exception, or a cancellation seen at any point before finalization (also after the work returns), rolls the group back and propagates. A document that already has an open transaction is refused before any work, because the group would own nothing to roll back. The work must complete inside the callback, where its gate calls run inline. Work still pending when the callback returns is canceled and the group is rolled back. The outcome is classified by the group status Revit reports: only RolledBack counts as discarded and only Committed as kept. Any other status throws TransactionGroupOutcomeUnknownException, and the caller must not report the work as discarded. Progress overlay Hosts Host tool views through ToolWindowFactory and IToolWindowSession. The modal and modeless shells expose the WPF owner. Core installs WindowInitializer before the XAML loads and retires its state with the session. Bind an overlay to its window with ProgressOverlay.For(window, logger), on the owner's UI thread. State, dispatcher affinity and diagnostics stay tied to that window. The logger is required. ProgressOverlayWindowCapability (ProgressOverlayWindowCapability.Hosts.cs) is the only registry from Window to overlay state and visual host. There is no ambient or process-global host. ProgressOverlay.Operations.cs holds the public lifecycle API. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow.cs owns RunAsync(...): the show policy, the linked cancellation source, cancel observation and hide sequencing. ProgressOverlayDelayedHideScheduler keeps the dispatcher operation it posts and observes every outcome. It clears the pending hide only when the completing operation owns the current cancellation source, so an aborted or faulted stale operation cannot clear a replacement hide. IProgressOverlay Member Behavior Show(title, cancelable) Shows the overlay and resets the cancellation state. Update(status, progress01) Sets status text and progress in [0,1]. A null argument leaves that value unchanged. A non-finite progress value throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException before status or progress changes. Finite values are clamped to [0,1]. UpdateStep(current, total, description, progress01) Sets the status to Step X/Y: {description}. Scope(title, cancelable) Returns a disposable scope. Nested scopes restore the parent state in LIFO order. CancelRequested Thread-safe snapshot of the Cancel button state. RequestCancel() Sets CancelRequested. Hide() Hides the overlay and clears transient state. RunAsync(title, work, cancelable, options, ct) Runs work with an overlay lifecycle and cancellation bridge. A second run on the same window while one is active throws InvalidOperationException. ProgressOverlay marshals public calls to its owner's WPF dispatcher. Do not change overlay state directly from a background thread. Pure and view-model tests can use a simple IProgressOverlay double. Rendering A status change forces a render (RequestRender(force: true)); a progress-only update is throttled. Phase changes stay visible when Revit starves the dispatcher. ProgressOverlayRenderScheduler throttles render requests to one per 30 ms and pumps one dispatcher frame (DispatcherFramePump.TryPumpSingleFrame) with a 20 ms budget and a depth guard. A forced render bypasses the pending-render guard. A pending render older than 250 ms is treated as stuck and replaced. Do not add other dispatcher pump loops or dispatcher-frame code outside that helper while Revit work is active. Cancellation Use RunAsync(...) for long operations. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow observes CancelRequested, cancels a linked token source and passes the work delegate a token that fires on cancel. After Show(...) resets the cancellation state, the cancel watcher starts before the work begins. SGT analysis (AnalysisSessionWorkflow), SGT placement (PlacementWorkflow) and GM commit review (CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow) use RunAsync. A workflow that drives its own Scope(...) reads CancelRequested and bridges it to its own cancellation. TDV transfer does this: its reporter returns Overlay.CancelRequested as IsCancellationRequested. using (Overlay.Scope("Transferring Drafting Views", cancelable: true)) { result = await _session.ApplySelectionAsync(items, reporter, CancellationToken.None); } Progress values Tools report IProgress<(string message, double? progress01)>: a status message and an optional fraction in [0,1]. MonotonicProgressAdapter (src/DBTools.Core/Progress/Aggregation) wraps such a reporter and forwards non-decreasing values clamped to [0,1]. A null fraction forwards the status and does not change the tracked value. A non-finite fraction throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException and does not change the tracked value. Create one adapter per operation. Tool Progress source Overlay mapping GM MappingPlanExecutor reports per-writer progress (writerIndex / writerCount); MappingApplyState.ReportProgress(message, progress01) reports within a writer. CommitReviewApplyWorkflow wraps the reporter in MonotonicProgressAdapter; CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow updates the overlay. TDV The transfer executor reports per-view stage percentages (0, 10, 25, 35, 60, 85, 100). TdvWindowViewModel.UpdateTransferOverlayProgress maps them through six weighted stages and never decreases. SGT PlacementExecutor.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync report wall-level and sub-step progress. PlacementWorkflow wraps the overlay in MonotonicProgressAdapter. Record Set ExecutionPlanExecutor.ExecuteAsync takes an Action<int> percentage and an Action<string> log. PlanExecutionWorkflow combines the last percentage with each log message in one overlay update. Common failures Dispatcher errors or missing state: an overlay call on a window that Core WindowInitializer did not initialize, or a change that bypasses the overlay API. Invalid Revit API context: Revit API calls outside IRevitCallGate, or async delegates inside the gate.

developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.title: Sandbox Validator | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.summary: Sandbox Validator DBTools.Sandbox validates one staged product year outside a running Revit session. It checks the candidate files, metadata and manifests, then builds the real tool windows and checks themes, layout, bindings and Dispatcher cleanup. It is also a host for developing tool UI with design-time view models. Sandbox is a Windows WPF executable (DBTools.Sandbox.exe, win-x64). Both modes need the matching Revit year installed: Sandbox resolves AdWindows.dll, RevitAPI.dll, RevitAPIUI.dll and UIFramework.dll from the Revit installation directory. Synopsis DBTools.Sandbox [--headless] [--dist-dir DIR] [--revit-reference-dir DIR] Option Description --headless Run the full validation sequence, close every window and exit with the result. Without it, Sandbox opens the window catalog for interactive use. Requires --revit-reference-dir. --dist-dir DIR A year directory (for example .artifacts/dist/Release/2026) or a distribution root that contains year directories. Default: .artifacts/dist/Release of the repository that contains the executable, else of the current directory. --revit-reference-dir DIR A directory with the four Revit reference files for the year. Their metadata must be compatible with the installed runtime. Valid only with --headless. Both --option VALUE and --option=VALUE are accepted. An empty value, an unknown argument or a missing value is an error. Without --headless, Sandbox uses the installed Revit runtime as the reference. A --dist-dir of the form /mnt/<drive>/... is converted to a Windows path. Examples, in PowerShell on Windows after ./build.sh BuildAll. Validate the 2026 candidate against the installed Revit 2026 files: .\.artifacts\sandbox\Release\2026\net10.0-windows\DBTools.Sandbox.exe --headless ` --dist-dir .artifacts\dist\Release\2026 ` --revit-reference-dir 'C:\Program Files\Autodesk\Revit 2026' Open the window catalog for the 2026 candidate: .\.artifacts\sandbox\Release\2026\net10.0-windows\DBTools.Sandbox.exe ` --dist-dir .artifacts\dist\Release\2026 The exit status is 0 when headless validation passes and 1 when it fails. A failure before WPF starts is written to standard error. Process model Each year runs in a new process in the default load context: SandboxEntry uses only BCL types. It parses the options, resolves the year directory and runs SandboxCandidate.Validate. A non-inlined method prepares the Revit runtime resolver and loads HandyControl, Presentation, Core, App and the manifest-declared tools from their candidate paths. A second non-inlined method starts the WPF application. The JIT compiles this call only after the candidate assemblies are loaded, so Core and WPF cannot resolve from anywhere else first. The process exits after validation, so no assembly of one candidate stays loaded for another year. Sandbox creates no load context, does not run App's Revit startup, does not load Revit reference files as product assemblies and does not probe subfolders other than Tools/. Candidate contract A candidate is one year directory of the product tree. SandboxCandidate checks the add-in file, the top-level files, the flat Tools/ directory, the PE simple names, and conflicts with assemblies already loaded in the process. No third-party DLL may be present. Validation sequence Resolve the year directory and the optional Revit reference directory. Check DBTools.addin, the exact top-level files, the recursive Tools/ files, the supported year and framework, and the PE simple names. Read the App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool references and their source-derived versions from PE metadata, without loading Revit API assemblies. Discover the embedded manifests and validate module, command, availability, icon, raw XAML and design-time view model ownership. Load the resources and themes, build the window catalog and each tool window, run layout and interaction checks, capture binding errors, close every window and verify Dispatcher cleanup. Fail if any Revit API assembly is loaded at the end. Portable validation of a distribution archive checks the same file set and also file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. Components Component Responsibility SandboxEntry BCL-only option parsing, year selection, candidate check and the non-inlined WPF start SandboxCandidate Candidate files, direct image loading, PE identity and loaded-image path checks SandboxDistributionContext References to the candidate's App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool assemblies and manifests ManifestValidator Manifest owners, commands, availability types, raw resources and design-time view models AssemblyMetadataInspector PE metadata and reference identities, read from bytes without running Revit code HeadlessValidationWorkflow The headless sequence and its structured result ToolWindowValidator Window construction, layout, interaction, binding errors and cleanup The portable manifest rules are in testing/DBTools.Distribution.Validation/Manifest/PortableToolManifestValidator.cs. Tool window registration A tool lists its Sandbox windows in manifest.yml: sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolView.xaml" windowKind: Modal designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public windowKind is Modal or Modeless. SandboxCatalog (Core) reads these entries into window specifications, and Sandbox hosts each raw view in the stable Presentation ToolWindowHost. No candidate Window type crosses between assemblies. Validation requires, for each entry: a nonempty id, displayName, group, xamlResource, designTimeViewModelType and designTimeViewModelAssembly; an EmbeddedResource in the owning project with exactly that LogicalName; a root element that derives from FrameworkElement and is not a Window; the host supplies the window shell; no x:Class, x:ClassModifier or x:FieldModifier, no code-behind event attributes, no CLR namespaces of the tool assembly, no implicit templates for tool types, no inferred DataGrid columns and no pack URIs into the tool assembly; a concrete design-time view model whose visibility matches designTimeViewModelVisibility (Public or Internal) and that has a parameterless constructor (public for Public); Sandbox invokes it. Give it fixed display data and no Revit, network or settings services. Tool code can check DBTools.Core.Sandbox.SandboxMode.IsActive to avoid services that do not exist in Sandbox. Every manifest command type must implement IExternalCommand and every availability type IExternalCommandAvailability, in the declared owner assembly under Tools/. Window checks ToolWindowValidator opens each raw view through ToolWindowHost with its design-time view model and then: measures and arranges the window at a fixed size and at infinite size; selects every tab of each TabControl and restores the original tab; shows the row details of the first three rows of each nonempty DataGrid, except grids whose details are VisibleWhenSelected; records WPF binding errors; closes the window and waits for a bounded ApplicationIdle Dispatcher barrier. It fails when the Dispatcher is missing, shutting down or aborted, or when a cleanup operation is still pending after the barrier. Build output and archives Sandbox is built once per year, although both years use the same framework: .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ build output sandbox/<year>/<sanitized-tfm>/ path inside the validation archive ./build.sh PackageSandboxValidationInput writes a content-addressed validate-dist-<sha256>.zip with the candidate and Sandbox. The DIST suite consumes that archive and writes a structured result JSON (see Distribution acceptance). The archive and the result keep normalized relative paths. The portable validation of the archive runs on any host and checks files and metadata only. The Windows acceptance suite runs DBTools.Sandbox.exe --headless for each year, with the reference files the archive carries under revit-refs/<year>/, so the window checks run there. Troubleshooting Failure Where to look Candidate file missing or extra ProductOutput staging and DistributionContract .addin entry mismatch build/Installer/DBTools.addin and the App output Tool assembly missing The manifest assembly name and Tools/ staging Raw XAML resource missing EmbeddedResource LogicalName in the owning project Design-time view model cannot be created Its visibility, designTimeViewModelVisibility and parameterless constructor Binding errors Explicit bindings and the stable Presentation templates Layout failure ToolWindowValidator measure and arrange messages Cleanup timeout Dispatcher and window owner lifetime A window failure reports both the primary exception and any cleanup exception. See Sandbox Integration, Assembly Loading Contract and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/structural-.title: Structural Preview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/structural-.summary: Structural Preview DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview is the stable WPF host for the structural 3D preview shared by the Extreme Roof Framing Tool (ERFT) and the Super Girt Tool (SGT). A tool adapter supplies immutable scene data and receives pointer events. The host owns the Helix viewport, effects manager, camera, navigation, materials, hit testing, tooltip, overlay markers and cleanup. Helix and SharpDX are merged into Presentation as internal types; no tool assembly or raw view names them. ERFT and SGT register the presenter's disposal with their tool-window sessions. The component has no Core, App or tool-assembly dependency. Its public scene records contain only immutable arrays, System.Numerics values, strings, integers and scalar values. Attach and dispose Call StructuralPreview3DFactory.Attach on the viewport host dispatcher. The ContentControl must be empty. The optional overlay canvas must use the same dispatcher.
