The returned IStructuralPreview3D owns one viewport and one effects manager. All presenter methods and disposal are synchronous UI-thread operations. Attach returns a disabled presenter without loading or creating Helix objects when StructuralPreview3DOptions.Disabled is true, and returns one with the load error as its reason when the Helix libraries cannot be loaded. The disabled presenter still validates and copies supplied scene and emphasis data, reports its status reason, returns false from projection, and can be disposed repeatedly. For an available presenter, Dispose removes viewport, camera, owner-window, timer and input handlers; closes the tooltip; removes only the overlay children created by this presenter; disposes owned scene elements, viewport and effects manager; clears scene data and subscriber events; and clears the host content only when that content is still the viewport owned by this presenter. Cleanup is synchronous and does not post a dispatcher frame. Disposal clears subscriptions before cleanup, so it publishes zero presenter events during or after disposal. Repeated disposal is safe. Scene data and picks SetScene validates and deep-copies the supplied records and arrays. The caller may then release or reuse its own objects. Equal mesh geometry keeps existing Helix models; geometry or appearance changes update the rendered decorations and materials, while bounds or exterior-normal changes update camera state. Mesh Opacity supplies the material alpha and overrides the alpha byte in Argb. Line sets multiply their ARGB alpha by Opacity. Selection and hover colors preserve the mesh opacity. Mesh picking is independent of emphasis. A mesh is eligible for a hit only when its supplied IsPickable value is true; context meshes can therefore be pickable or non-pickable independently of their material role. A floor is supplied as scene geometry, normally a context mesh with IsPickable: false. Line sets and non-pickable meshes do not produce mesh hits. A missed hit has null mesh ID, null context ID and null world point. A hit's mesh and context hits are resolved independently: each is the nearest eligible hit for its role. MeshId is the nearest member ID, or null when there is no member hit; ContextId is the nearest context ID independently. WorldPoint is the nearest member hit point when one exists, otherwise the context hit point, so a context-only hit has a null mesh ID and a context world point. The event also carries WPF screen coordinates relative to the viewport and keyboard modifiers. SetEmphasis accepts one emphasis state per mesh ID. The presenter applies selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover material policies from the selected StructuralPreviewPalette. StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt and .Erft are the adapter presets. They differ in member color boost, surfaces, selection and hover colors, and edge and outline settings, and use the same renderer. The presenter adds a pivot marker to the supplied overlay canvas while orbiting. The marker and all generated WPF objects have their data context cleared or blocked so tool data contexts do not flow into the stable visual tree. Home views and camera movement The ExteriorThreeQuarter strategy is the SGT home view. When bounds or the exterior normal changes, the session recomputes and stores a raw Home camera. Its exact formula is: distance = max(2.2 * boundsDiagonal, 8) yaw = 28 degrees pitch = 0.22 downward along the configured up axis The exterior normal is projected onto the up plane. A missing horizontal normal uses negative Y as the stable fallback. The stored Home keeps this exact distance. Clamping applies to the displayed camera only. If the user has moved the camera, a changed scene clamps the current camera and retains the new raw Home for a later reset. Reset clears the moved flag, applies Home, and clamps the displayed camera. ERFT uses the PreserveAngle strategy. When bounds change, the session fits the current view angle and captures that result as Home. The fit formula is: halfV = radians(fieldOfView) / 2 halfH = atan(tan(halfV) * aspect) distance = max(boundsDiagonal / 2 / sin(min(halfV, halfH)), 2) * 1.2 Helix FieldOfView is the vertical angle. The fit keeps the bounds' bounding sphere inside both the vertical and the horizontal field of view, so the whole scene is visible at the viewport aspect when the fit runs; the distance clamp still applies. Scene constraints use these bounds-only constants (StructuralPreviewCameraMath): diagonal = actualDiagonal, or 10 when actualDiagonal <= 1e-6 min = clamp(diagonal * 0.0005, 0.005, 0.75) max = clamp(diagonal * 40, min * 2, 50000) targetPad = max(2, diagonal * 6) near = max(0.0005, min * 0.05) far = max(100, max * 2) When a scene changes mesh geometry without changing these bounds, the presenter keeps the stored Home object and only updates its owned render models. Adapters must compute bounds from every mesh vertex so a real extent change is reported as a bounds change; a bounds change is an intentional Home refit under PreserveAngle. ZoomToFit performs the exact fit. When FitRedefinesHome is enabled, the fitted camera becomes Home and the viewport default camera is updated to the same pose; otherwise the fit marks the camera as user-moved while preserving Home. ResetView restores stored Home. Pan uses screen-space camera axes, orbit uses the configured arbitrary up axis around the selected or picked pivot, and wheel zoom moves toward the picked world anchor. Gesture cancellation occurs on lost capture, window deactivation, unload and disabled interaction. The viewport's native view cube handles its own preview input before scene picking. The presenter keeps the default camera synchronized with stored scene Home when a scene is attached; an explicit fit also updates it when FitRedefinesHome is enabled. Input and hover StructuralPreview3DOptions.ShowTooltips defaults to true. It enables the stable presenter's mesh tooltips. When disabled, pointer updates keep the tooltip closed. Materials and lighting Adapters choose StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt or .Erft and can copy the record to adjust individual values. A palette supplies member and context surfaces, key/fill/rim/ambient light colors, sibling and dimmed policies, selection and hover colors, emissive scaling, edge colors and thickness, outline mode and pivot colors. IsPickable controls hit testing. A non-pickable context mesh remains rendered with its base context material but bypasses selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover emphasis; pickable context meshes can receive context hover, sibling and dimmed states but never member selection states. The SGT preset uses these alpha rules. Sibling emphasis scales diffuse alpha by 0.70 and retains the source ambient, specular and emissive alpha. Dimmed emphasis sets every channel's alpha to max(0.05, sourceAlpha * 0.45). Hovering a sibling restores the base material and adds emissive brightness while preserving its source alpha. Hovering a dimmed mesh adds emissive brightness and retains the dimmed alpha. The default options select the SGT palette and exterior home strategy. ERFT selects both its palette and its camera strategy: var options = new StructuralPreview3DOptions { Palette = StructuralPreviewPalette.Erft, HomeView = StructuralPreviewHomeView.PreserveAngle }; Diagnostics and projection Diagnostic reports debug, warning and error messages as plain strings with an optional exception. Repeated identical diagnostic messages are suppressed for two seconds. An initialization or disabled-path diagnostic is delivered once to the first diagnostic subscriber; the reason is also available in Status. Event publication takes an invocation-list snapshot and stops when a callback disposes the presenter. No presenter event is raised after Dispose clears subscriptions. On the first render failure, the presenter changes to Unavailable, disables interaction, cancels navigation, clears hover state, stops its clamp timer and collapses the viewport. It reports that failure as an error diagnostic, subject to the two-second diagnostic de-duplication; later render failures are ignored while the presenter is unavailable. TryProjectToViewport returns false when the presenter is unavailable, disposed, unloaded, has no render context, receives a non-finite point, has an invalid camera or the point is behind the camera. It returns WPF device- independent coordinates relative to the viewport on success. Projection failures are reported as debug diagnostics and never escape as exceptions. Public API The following declarations are the public API. developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.title: Test Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.summary: Test Pipeline This page describes how DB Tools tests are selected, staged and run. For the test.sh options, examples and the rules for writing tests, see Testing Tools. DB Tools tests run through one of two routes: ./test.sh resolves the selected projects, builds them, freezes their inputs and runs them locally or submits them to the dbtools-daemon fleet. It writes the receipts that --no-build and CI consume. See the test.sh command reference. Plain dotnet test on an entry project in testing/Daemon/ uses the pinned daemon VSTest adapter (DbToolsDaemon.RevitTest.TestAdapter). MSBuild builds the selected assemblies, models, includes and per-year sources, and the adapter submits them in one request. See Daemon adapter entry projects. Use one route per invocation. Both read the relay URL from DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL; the daemon owns relay credentials, and neither route accepts or stores them. Scopes and suites Scope or suite Marker Where it runs Pure tests (pure) plain [Test] Without Revit. Locally when possible; otherwise as a daemon PureSuite job on a hidden Windows desktop Revit-hosted tests (local) [RevitLocal] Inside Revit on a daemon worker, for one selected year Design Automation tests (da) [RevitDA] On the invoking host, as an HTTP client of APS Design Automation; never through the daemon DIST The Windows distribution acceptance suite, always a daemon PureSuite job BUILD Linux-native build and distribution contract suites Revit-hosted tests exercise the real ribbon, WPF and add-in lifecycle in Revit. Design Automation tests build the Revit 2026 Sentinel WorkItem test project and run it with dotnet test; see APS Design Automation Sentinel. Pure requests have no year. A Revit-hosted request for two years makes one daemon request per year, each with its own product tree and report. Design Automation tests always build Revit 2026. Selection test.sh list --projects prints the sorted scope<TAB>project rows and is the source of truth for what a request selects. It evaluates project membership, explicit Compile Include, Exclude and Remove items, disabled default items, NUnit fixture attributes and the selected tool, scope and year. The same index resolves fixtures and exact FQNs. A fixture must resolve to one compiled owner class. An unknown fixture or project, an unreadable project or source file, a project the selected tool and scope cannot reach, or an explicit scope with no resolved project exits with status 2 before any build or submission. An exact FullyQualifiedName=<FQN> filter becomes an exact daemon selector, and a prefix filter becomes a prefix selector. A Revit-hosted filter that cannot be mapped exits with status 2 instead of selecting the whole assembly. Pure routing test.sh checks each selected Pure assembly for its .deps.json, .runtimeconfig.json and the output-local NUnit3.TestAdapter.dll, then routes it: to the daemon if it is the DIST suite or a machine is pinned; to the daemon if it targets Windows and the host is not Windows; to the daemon if the host lacks Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App; a missing other framework is an error; otherwise to local VSTest. Projects that run locally, including the Linux BUILD and Distribution suites, run one after another; daemon submissions run concurrently, at most DBT_PURE_CONCURRENCY (default 2) at a time. A local project that runs zero tests fails. With a filter expression, the run fails only when no selected project runs a test. Linux-native BUILD projects and *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects are skipped on Windows with a notice. Inputs and receipts For a selected scope and year, the MSBuild graph returns the test assembly, target framework, model items and product-tree includes in one pass. Before any submission, test.sh freezes the assemblies, runtime closure, product-tree includes, models and companions into the content-addressed test input cache (DBT_TEST_INPUT_CACHE_ROOT), so a later build cannot change the submitted files. A normal exit removes the per-run directory. --compile-only writes a receipt bound to the source identity, the selected projects, the graph inputs and the output hashes. --no-build verifies all of these and refuses stale or missing files. CI resolves the selectors once with ./test.sh list --projects, compiles each selected scope with --compile-only, transfers the receipt and the recorded input closure, and runs them with --no-build. The consumer never rebuilds. Linux BUILD and DIST jobs do not depend on the Windows transfer. The build and distribution suites read already-built product metadata and reject a stale source snapshot. Source, build and test changes alter the snapshot; documentation and transient artifacts do not. Results The daemon terminal JSON is the result. After a zero submit exit, the summary must report result_status=passed, a positive passed count, and zero failed, errored, and aborted counts. Skipped tests can accompany passed tests. Zero executed tests, including an all-skipped run, fail admission. A nonzero submit exit is kept even when the terminal JSON is missing or malformed. When retrieval succeeds, failed runs keep their reports and original exit status. Rejected terminal summaries are saved as *.invalid-summary.json. Full report retrieval accepts a report exit of zero or the submit exit. The report file must be nonempty, and its JSON request identity, status, and counts must match the accepted summary. Retrieval makes three report attempts, stopping after the first accepted report. Two one-second delays separate three failed attempts. It never resubmits tests. Only an accepted report is published to the result path. After exhaustion, nonempty rejected output is saved as PATH.invalid-report.json, where PATH is the full report path. The wrapper keeps a nonzero submit exit or returns 2 after a zero submit exit. Independent scopes in one request continue after a failure, but test.sh returns the first nonzero status. Daemon adapter entry projects testing/Daemon/Hosted/<Tool>.Hosted.Entry.csproj builds DBTools.<Tool>.Local.Tests for both years (Hosted2026.proj, Hosted2027.proj). The App and Core entries also build DBTools.<Tool>.HostedTurns.Local.Tests. testing/Daemon/Pure/<Tool>.Pure.Entry.csproj selects every DBTools.<Tool>.*Pure.Tests.csproj beside its owner. After the build, the entry writes dbtools-daemon.runsettings from Hosted.runsettings or Pure.runsettings with the literal sources, models and includes. The hosted settings default to years 2026,2027, isolated execution and a 30-minute timeout, and treat a run with no tests as an error. Product staging Each Revit-hosted test for a year receives the product tree that the installer uses, under product/<year>/. The tree keeps its relative paths. Test assemblies and NUnit and adapter dependencies are separate inputs. App loads tools from Tools/ by explicit path into the context that holds it, so ProductLoadContext and DevModeLoadContext receive the same identities as the staged tree. Test support installs no resolver for product assemblies. Test projects Test projects are next to their production owners: src/DBTools.App/Tests/DBTools.App.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Core/Tests/DBTools.Core.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Sandbox/Tests/DBTools.Sandbox.Pure.Tests.csproj src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/Tests/DBTools.<Tool>.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj testing/DBTools.Build.Tests/ build and distribution contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Tests/ portable archive contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Windows.Tests/ DIST suite testing/RevitTestModels/ test models by year and tool An owner has both a .Pure.Tests and a .Local.Tests project only when both kinds of test exist. Pure projects list their source files explicitly and reference their normal production owners. Shared props give every Pure project $(DBT_PureRevitYear) (2026) and static graph restore, and pass that year on owner references, so a plain dotnet build or dotnet test of one project needs no properties. Revit is compile-only in Pure tests: a test must not load Revit-typed members or scan owner types outside the loadable set. .Local.Tests projects disable default compile items and include only Revit-hosted fixtures. Presentation behavior tests are under Presentation; the Core Pure projects link the fixtures they can run without Revit. Tests that need a real WPF window run where Windows is available. Portable Pure projects Core and the Super Girt Tool (SGT) define an optional $(DBT_PortableTargetFramework). Their *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects build against that framework and run on Linux; CI and Windows test.sh route them to Linux. To make a project portable: declare desktop and portable TargetFrameworks; condition DBT_RevitHostIdentity, UseWPF and the Presentation ProjectReference on the desktop framework, and keep Revit references under the desktop host identity condition; set DBT_UsesMergedAssemblies=false in portable consumers. build/MSBuild/Portable.targets excludes App, Revit, Views, DesignTime and XAML inputs. Portable images use ordinary NuGet dependencies, have no content version and add no staged runtime files. Core uses an explicit list of source files for its portable build. Test models Revit-hosted projects declare RevitTestModel items relative to testing/RevitTestModels: testing/RevitTestModels/ ├── 2026/GM/gm_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/sgt_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/_LinkedModels/sgt_test_linked_model.rvt ├── 2026/Regression/realtest_model.rvt ├── 2027/... (same layout) ├── GM/SharedParameters/shared_parameters.txt └── VTC/vtc_import_layers.dxf Model files and explicit non-RVT inputs keep their relative paths in the daemon stage. Revit-hosted fixtures find them under DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_MODELS_DIR; Pure fixtures use the repository root in DBT_TEST_REPO_ROOT. TestPathResolver reads the root on every call, so a job never sees the model root of a previous job. A fixture may open a temporary copy of a model, but the daemon owns the active document and the worker lifecycle. Models resolve only from these roots, not from a worker checkout or an %APPDATA% cache. Test support testing/TestSupport holds shared test infrastructure and doubles for true externals. Tool-specific doubles are under testing/TestSupport/<Tool> and are linked as source by the matching test projects; they are not a separate assembly. Revit/RevitHost.cs initializes the year, the App runtime and the product Revit call gate before the test body, and supplies the real UIApplication through an ambient scope that does not carry API access across an await. It owns the scheduler unless a fixture holds a longer lease. Forced-queue tests call the real external-event handler synchronously to model a later API turn; one daemon NUnit callback contains no second native turn. Wpf/WpfTestRuntimeBootstrap.cs registers pack URI support, installs the shared window owner, validates themes in the runtime assembly's contextual reflection scope, and releases only its own provider at teardown. It adds no Resolving handlers and does not force Presentation or HandyControl into the default context. Logging/TestLoggingBridge.cs uses production logging when Revit provides it and a console and file host otherwise. Revit-hosted fixtures release only their own runtime, Revit task, owner handle and window resources. Cleanup reports both the primary failure and any cleanup failure. See Build Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.title: Theme System | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.summary: Theme System DBTools.Presentation.dll holds every compiled WPF resource of the product: the theme dictionaries, stable controls and window shells. It stays loaded for the life of the Revit process. Tool views are raw XAML that Presentation parses at run time, so App, Core and the tool assemblies contain no BAML and no .g.resources. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, never into Application.Resources, so DB Tools does not change the appearance of other add-ins. Assembly roles Assembly Compiled WPF content DBTools.Presentation Theme dictionaries, stable windows and controls, tool behaviors and converters under Tools/<TOOL>/, the merged Helix theme, and the settings views of DialogSuppression, ElevationTags, FoundationTags and JoistGirderWeight (linked from those tool folders) DBTools.HandyControl The HandyControl skins and themes DBTools.Core None. Window lifecycle, error boundaries, registry, commands and runtime hosts can be reloaded Tool assemblies None. Tool views are embedded as raw XAML Presentation keeps explicit Page, Compile and EmbeddedResource items (EnableDefaultPageItems=false). The linked tool settings views keep their tool namespaces, for example DBTools.DialogSuppression.Settings.Views; the tool projects remove them from their own Page items. Tool views A tool embeds each view as an EmbeddedResource with the logical name DBTools.ToolViews.<TOOL>.<View>.xaml. ToolWindowFactory.Create (Core) opens a view in these steps: ToolWindowHost.Create (Presentation) creates a stable shell, ToolWindowModalShell or ToolWindowModelessShell. The shell initializer runs before the view is parsed. The default is WindowInitializer.Initialize or InitializeModeless, which applies the theme, binds the owner window, registers the progress overlay and installs the error boundary and logging. ToolWindowXaml.LoadElement parses the raw view inside ToolWindowReflectionScope, and the view and shell receive the tool's view model as DataContext. The factory registers the session in ToolWindowRegistry. The caller shows the window with session.ShowDialog() or session.Show() and gets named controls with session.Require<T>(name). The Settings, Alert, Logger and notification banner windows are raw resources in Presentation and use the same loader; so do tool template dictionaries such as the View Template Comparer (VTC) diff templates and the Super Girt Tool (SGT) opening view. For these windows Core keeps the state, commands and lifecycle and event handling; the controls need no typed constructor from a reloadable assembly and do no type discovery at run time. Retirement tears down bindings, automation roots, resources and callbacks. Core lifecycle handlers are released through BehaviorState and session cleanup before the shell closes. A custom shell initializer releases its own handles. Raw views name only framework types or public stable Presentation types and merge the theme through Presentation's ResourceUri markup extension before they use static theme keys. Tool content uses explicit keyed templates. SGT's opening and girt grids use stable behaviors over tool row state. The Extreme Roof Framing Tool (ERFT) and SGT pass immutable scene data to the stable 3D viewport, which owns camera, material, picking and device state (see Structural Preview). Theme dictionaries The root dictionary is: /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Theme.xaml <PresentationVersion> is the content version of the Presentation assembly (see Build Pipeline). The root merges, in this order: /DBTools.HandyControl;V<HandyControlVersion>;component/Themes/SkinDark.xaml /DBTools.HandyControl;V<HandyControlVersion>;component/Themes/Theme.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Tokens.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Brushes.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Converters.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Controls.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/DataGrid.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Menus.xaml /DBTools.Presentation;V<PresentationVersion>;component/Resources/Components.xaml ThemeResourceLoader (Core) checks this order. At startup ThemeValidator.ValidateOrThrow registers the pack URI scheme, loads each dictionary separately and freezes its freezables, loads the root and checks its merged dictionaries, and then measures and arranges a probe tree of standard controls. A failure stops startup; see Troubleshooting. Resource URIs Every compiled resource URI contains the assembly's version. A changed stable assembly therefore has a new identity, and WPF cannot select an older copy of Presentation or HandyControl that an earlier DB Tools version has already loaded. Presentation URIs use the Presentation version, and HandyControl URIs use the HandyControl version. The component URI is relative, so Application.LoadComponent does not need the pack scheme to be registered. Use ResourceUri.CreateResourceUri for Application.LoadComponent, dictionary sources and the dictionary markup extensions. Use ResourceUri.CreateAbsoluteResourceUri for images and icons created in code without a WPF base URI. It registers the pack scheme and returns pack://application:,,,/<assembly>;V<version>;component/<path>. WindowInitializer loads the window icon with BitmapCacheOption.OnLoad inside its warning boundary; otherwise WPF can defer the file lookup until it creates the window handle. XAML namespaces XAML outside Presentation refers to stable types with clr-namespace:...;assembly=DBTools.Presentation. XAML compiled by Presentation uses the namespace form without assembly=. This keeps the BAML compiler from resolving Presentation types through a reloadable assembly. BAML assembly versions The BAML assembly table must contain the final assembly version, because WPF resolves local markup extensions through that table separately from the outer pack URI. Keep SDK assembly-info generation on in WPF temporary projects. With it off, BAML references Version=0.0.0.0; if an older Presentation is already loaded in the default context, the CLR can satisfy that request with the older copy. That copy lacks HandyControlResourceUriExtension, and WPF throws NotImplementedException before it opens the HandyControl dictionaries. WPF's local-assembly fallback runs only when loading throws, so a successful bind to the older copy bypasses it. See .NET 10 WPF assembly and type resolution and CoreCLR version compatibility. Source files File Responsibility src/DBTools.Presentation/DBTools.Presentation.csproj Assembly identity and the explicit list of compiled pages and embedded views src/DBTools.Presentation/Resources/Theme.xaml Root theme dictionary src/DBTools.Presentation/Resources/ResourceUri.cs Versioned resource URIs src/DBTools.Core/UI/Theming/ThemeResource/ThemeResourceLoader.cs Merge order check src/DBTools.Core/UI/Theming/ThemeValidator.cs Startup theme validation src/DBTools.App/DBTools.App.csproj App resources and embedded manifests; no tool XAML build/Distribution/DistributionContract.cs The product file list See DBTools.Presentation, Project References and Assembly Loading Contract.

developer-guide/architecture/wiki-server.title: Wiki Server | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/wiki-server.summary: Wiki Server wiki/server-config/ holds the configuration of the web server that serves this documentation site at https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net. The server runs Caddy for the static files and a webhook container that updates them. A push to the main branch of the kirsch33/dbtools-wiki repository makes the server pull the new site. Publishing flow The Documentation workflow (.github/workflows/documentation.yml, manual dispatch) builds the site with .github/scripts/build-docs.sh and pushes wiki/_site to the main branch of kirsch33/dbtools-wiki. It authenticates with the deploy key in the WIKI_DEPLOY_KEY secret. GitHub sends the push event of kirsch33/dbtools-wiki to https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net/hooks/dbtools-wiki, signed with the shared secret in the X-Hub-Signature-256 header. Caddy proxies /hooks/* to the webhook container on port 9000. The dbtools-wiki hook runs only when the HMAC-SHA256 signature is valid, repository.full_name is kirsch33/dbtools-wiki and ref is refs/heads/main. It then runs /scripts/pull-site.sh dbtools-wiki. pull-site.sh reads the site entry from sites.json. On first use it clones the branch with depth 1 into the web directory; after that it fetches the branch and runs git reset --hard origin/<branch>. Caddy serves /web/dbtools-wiki as static files. A path that matches no file or directory returns /index.html. Files File Content Dockerfile The webhook image: almir/webhook, pinned by digest, plus bash, git and jq. It runs as the base image's unprivileged webhook user. docker-compose.yml The webhook service: builds the image, runs webhook -verbose -template -hooks=/etc/webhook/hooks.json -hotreload, mounts config/ and scripts/ read-only and /web read-write, reads webhook.env, and joins the external caddy_default network. webhook.env.example Template for webhook.env, which sets WEBHOOK_SECRET. config/hooks.json The hook definitions. -template lets each hook read WEBHOOK_SECRET with getenv. config/sites.json Maps a site name to repo (GitHub owner/name), web_dir and branch (default main). scripts/pull-site.sh pull-site.sh <site-name>: clones or updates one site from sites.json. It exits with status 1 when the name is missing or unknown, or sites.json is absent. caddy-snippet.txt The Caddy site block for dbtools.greatwhitelab.net. hooks.json and sites.json also define a blog site (kirsch33/blog, served from /web/blog) that uses the same script. Requirements Docker with Compose, and a Caddy container on the external Docker network caddy_default. The image needs bash, git and jq, because pull-site.sh uses all three. The base image has only the webhook binary and /bin/sh; the Dockerfile adds them with apk. The host directory /web must be writable by the UID:GID in the user field of docker-compose.yml (1001:1001). Set it to the server user that owns the bind mounts. The site repository must be readable over anonymous HTTPS, because pull-site.sh clones https://github.com/<repo>.git without credentials. The GitHub webhook and webhook.env must use the same secret. Setup Copy webhook.env.example to webhook.env and set WEBHOOK_SECRET, for example from openssl rand -hex 32. Check and start the service: docker compose config --quiet docker compose up -d --build Add the block from caddy-snippet.txt to the Caddyfile and reload Caddy. On kirsch33/dbtools-wiki, add a webhook for push events with the payload URL https://dbtools.greatwhitelab.net/hooks/dbtools-wiki, the content type application/json and the same secret. -hotreload makes the webhook reload hooks.json when the file changes. A change to the Dockerfile needs docker compose up -d --build. To move to another base image, resolve its digest and rebuild on the wiki host.

developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.title: Feature Warnings | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/feature-warni.summary: Feature Warnings A feature warning reports an actionable configuration or prerequisite problem. Active warnings block the commands named by their definitions and publish ribbon enablement updates. Warning state lasts for the current runtime session. It is not persisted to settings. The Settings window displays warning cards. The Settings button shows a warning icon, and the DB Tools tab receives a highlight when warnings exist. Command preflight and contextual edit flows use the same registered warning policy as ribbon controls. Defining warnings in manifest.yml Declare warnings under a settings pack: tool: settingsPacks: - key: structural.foundation_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags" warnings: - id: core.structural.combined_tags title: "Combined Foundation Tags Disabled" message: "Use Settings -> Combined Foundation Tags -> Install/Repair. A successful repair clears the warning and re-enables the commands." disableTools: - DBTools.UpdateCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.MoveCombinedFoundationTags - DBTools.OrganizeFoundationTypes Property Requirement and meaning id Required globally unique warning identity. title Required warning-card title. message Required description and corrective action. disableTools Optional list of registered ribbon internalName values. Use stable IDs such as core.library.invalid, core.structural.elevation_tags, and core.structural.joist_girder. List only commands that depend on the prerequisite. Name the problem, the affected operation, and the correction in the warning message. ToolWarningManifest carries the ID, title, message, and disabled-tool list. The manifest is metadata. It does not activate the warning by itself. Registering warning definitions Register a warning as the Warning member of SettingsPackRegistration<TOptions,TContext> in ToolModule.RegisterSettingsPacks. Settings Packs contains the full registration, including the required typed SettingsSection. Warning = new SettingsPackWarningRegistration<SettingsPackContext> { Id = warning.Id, Title = warning.Title, Message = warning.Message, ToolInternalNamesToDisable = warning.DisableTools, FlagGetter = context => context.HasWarning, FlagSetter = (context, active) => context.HasWarning = active } SettingsPackWarningRegistration<TContext> exposes these members: Member Type Required Id, Title, Message string Yes ToolInternalNamesToDisable IReadOnlyCollection<string>? No FlagGetter Func<TContext, bool> Yes FlagSetter Action<TContext, bool> Yes The registration extension validates required values at runtime. The bound runtime warning retains the exact context created by its pack. Callers cannot supply another context to its getter or setter. The context owns HasWarning for presentation and editing. The settings DTO owns persisted preferences such as AutoUpdateEnabled. IAutoUpdateSettings requires only that preference. Do not serialize a warning flag or derive command blocking from a saved flag. Triggering warnings Tools use DBTools.Core.Settings.Warnings.ISettingsWarningService: IReadOnlyCollection<ISettingsWarningDefinition> Definitions { get; } bool IsWarningActive(string warningId); SettingsWarningStateChange SetWarning(string warningId, bool active); warnings.SetWarning("core.structural.combined_tags", true); if (warnings.IsWarningActive("core.structural.combined_tags")) return; Blank or unknown IDs fail. Definitions must exist in the validated settings catalog before a tool uses them. Warning lookup is ordinal and case-sensitive. SetWarning updates session state and publishes the warning and aggregate visual state. SettingsWarningStateChange reports the prior and current state. The concrete SettingsWarningService owns active-ID enumeration and replay. SettingsWarningPublicationPolicy publishes individual warning changes, full replay, and aggregate HasWarnings. Tools receive the narrowed public interface, not internal publication operations. Validation and activation A warning-aware editor implements ISettingsWarningContext.WarningId and returns an invalid SettingsValidationResult for a configuration problem. The ID must belong to that pack. Use the actual result API: public Task<SettingsValidationResult> ValidateAsync(CancellationToken ct = default) { ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested(); return Task.FromResult(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(LibraryPath) ? SettingsValidationResult.FromErrors("Select a library path.") : SettingsValidationResult.Success); } This excerpt checks an editor-owned LibraryPath. A real library validator must also check its required file/directory conditions. Conditional features can return Success when disabled if their configuration is unnecessary then. Do not report an unexpected I/O or programming exception as invalid settings. Validation has distinct publication rules: Operation Warning behavior Startup Load saved options into fresh runtimes without views. Activate invalid warning-aware packs. Do not proactively clear warnings. Open Settings Validate loaded options and publish warning state. Validate button Evaluate unsaved drafts and editor flags. Do not change shared command blocking. Save before commit Evaluate drafts and reject blocking invalid values. Do not publish draft decisions. Save after commit Validate saved values in fresh runtimes, project decisions, and replay published state. Reset Commit defaults, apply them, validate, and publish. ISettingsPackSaveValidation.BlockSaveOnInvalid determines whether an invalid draft blocks Save. Invalid settings and a validation exception are different outcomes. Startup logs a validation exception without activating its feature warning. Settings-window failures propagate through the normal error path. Startup disposes every runtime it creates. It retries a failed disposal once, logs persistent failures with the pack identity, and preserves cancellation when cleanup also fails. The warning evaluator uses the same validated SettingsCatalog as the Settings window. Auto-update task integration ViewActivationTask<TSettings> reads the current settings once during admission. It returns no admission when AutoUpdateEnabled is false or any configured warning is active. Otherwise it evaluates the tool predicate and returns an admission that captures that settings snapshot. The hook distinguishes two failures: An admission failure records a document-session failure and activates WarningIdsToSetOnFailure. A settings-read failure occurs at this boundary. A failure while executing an admitted operation shows the canonical auto-update failure banner and suppresses further runs for that document session. It does not activate feature warnings automatically. Tool-owned prerequisite checks can activate a warning explicitly, for example when required shared parameters are missing. Unexpected runtime exceptions must propagate to the hook's safe-execution boundary. See Hooks for admission, document-session identity, and failure handling. An active warning can disable the editor's toggle through ToggleEnabled. Changing the persisted AutoUpdateEnabled preference is a separate tool policy. It is not a required side effect of SetWarning. Warning UI and command blocking SettingsWarningViewModel wraps an ISettingsPackRuntimeWarning. It exposes WarningId, Title, Message, IsActive, Clear and Fix commands, and Fix availability. The warning card binds to that row state. Publication reaches ribbon controls in this order: The warning service publishes a WarningChangedEventArgs. RibbonSettingsObserver receives the published change. RibbonVisualUpdater applies its per-command enabled state. RibbonCompositionState updates registered buttons. RibbonComposer registers controls before subscribing to settings changes. RibbonVisualUpdater also applies aggregate Settings-icon and tab-highlight updates. RibbonSettingsObserver owns subscription lifetime and dispatcher delivery. RibbonCompositionState owns the registered controls and panel state. Command preflight checks every applicable active warning. Ribbon enablement instead applies each warning's latest update directly. If several warnings name one command, clearing one can visually enable its button while another still blocks execution. Give each disabled command one warning definition when its ribbon state must match command preflight. WarningChangedEventArgs carries WarningId, PackKey, IsActive, and ToolInternalNamesToDisable. WarningSetChangedEventArgs carries aggregate HasWarnings. Treat these as published state, not persistence requests. Clearing and fixing warnings Clear sets the bound context warning false and calls ISettingsWarningService.SetWarning(id, false). It does not repair prerequisites or save settings. A later validation or prerequisite check can activate the warning again. A tool can clear a warning programmatically after its prerequisite check succeeds: warnings.SetWarning("core.structural.combined_tags", false); Changing only a context property does not publish command availability. Use the service or the Settings validation workflow to synchronize published state. A context that implements IWarningFixProvider can add a Fix action: string FixWarningId { get; } string FixLabel { get; } Task FixWarningAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); The provider's warning ID must match the card. Blank IDs or labels fail construction. SettingsWarningViewModel invokes the provider, updates command state when the context changes, and logs action failures. Its ActionFailed event passes failures to Settings feedback. Disposal unsubscribes the context observer. Combined Foundation Tags uses Fix for Install/Repair and explicit refresh for shared parameter checks. Its constructor only prepares editor state. See Settings Packs for host context and persistence ordering. Examples Combined Foundation Tags uses core.structural.combined_tags for Update Combined Foundation Tags, Move Combined Tags, and Organize Foundation Types. Transfer Drafting Views (TDV) uses core.library.invalid for Import From Library and Export To Library. Joist Girder Weights uses core.structural.joist_girder for its update command. Their manifests under src/Tools/ define the IDs and messages. See Testing Tools for warning-service test procedures.

developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.title: Hooks | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/hooks.html.summary: Hooks Hooks attach tool behavior to Revit application events. Core's HookHost resolves registered implementations, owns the shared ViewActivated subscription, and coordinates initialization, rollback, and shutdown. Tool-owned lifecycle hooks manage subscriptions that need their own event adapters. Use IViewActivationTask for work triggered by a view change. Use IHookLifecycle for owned subscriptions such as contextual ribbon UI or dialog suppression. Register services through the tool module. Do not attach another copy of Core's ViewActivated handler. Hook architecture flowchart LR Revit[Revit events] --> Host[HookHost] Registry[ToolRegistry and DI] --> Host Host --> View[ViewActivationHook] Host --> Lifecycle[IHookLifecycle implementations] View --> Tasks[IViewActivationTask services] AppHooksToolModule registers the single ViewActivationHook service and its RegisterHook<ViewActivationHook, ViewActivationHook>() mapping. The hook collects IEnumerable<IViewActivationTask> from DI. ViewActivationHookDispatcher owns the outer safe-execution boundary. ViewActivationTaskRunner evaluates admissions and executes admitted tasks. HookCatalog accepts only ViewActivationHook and IHookLifecycle contracts. It resolves each registered implementation from the service provider and fails when a service is missing or does not implement its declared contract. New contracts require explicit catalog and host subscription support. Hooks run in response to Revit UI callbacks. Returning Task does not move API work to a background thread. Use asynchronous I/O where appropriate, avoid blocking the UI, and reacquire a valid Revit call gate before API work after an await. Modularity describes the synchronous callback restriction. Registering hooks Register both the concrete service and its hook mapping: public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { services.AddSingleton<ContextualEditHook>(); } public override void RegisterHooks(ToolRegistry registry, ToolManifest manifest) { registry.RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle, ContextualEditHook>(); } This excerpt assumes a tool-owned ContextualEditHook : IHookLifecycle whose constructor dependencies are registered. Manifest and module setup is described in Creating New Tools. View-activation tasks use a factory registration. The Elevation Tags task needs manifest warning IDs in addition to its registered service dependencies: var warning = manifest.GetSingleSettingsPack().GetSingleWarning(manifest.Id); var warningIds = new[] { warning.Id }; services.AddSingleton<ElevationTagsUpdater>(); services.AddSingleton<IViewActivationTask>(sp => new ViewActivatedTask( sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsProvider>(), sp.GetRequiredService<SettingsSection<ElevationTagsSettings>>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ISettingsWarningService>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ElevationTagsUpdater>(), sp.GetRequiredService<IErrorNotifier>(), sp.GetRequiredService<ILogger<ViewActivatedTask>>(), warningIds)); This excerpt follows Elevation Tags' App/Composition/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs. The IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds constructor argument comes from the manifest, not automatic DI resolution. Every task must have a nonblank unique TaskId. All entries in WarningIdsToSetOnFailure must match registered warning definitions. The task registry validates these identities at construction. The IViewActivationTask System The public contract separates admission from execution: public interface IViewActivationTask { string TaskId { get; } string DisplayName { get; } IReadOnlyCollection<string> WarningIdsToSetOnFailure { get; } Task<ViewActivationAdmission?> AdmitAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, CancellationToken ct); } AdmitAsync returns null to skip the attempt. A non-null ViewActivationAdmission captures the state that attempt will use: new ViewActivationAdmission(executionCt => ExecuteAsync(snapshot, executionCt)); The hook invokes the returned admission callback once for that attempt. Create a new admission for each event so it captures that event's state. ViewActivationTask Derive from ViewActivationTask<TSettings> for an auto-update task with typed settings. TSettings must implement IAutoUpdateSettings and have a public parameterless constructor. Its base constructor receives: ViewActivationTask( ISettingsProvider settingsProvider, SettingsSection<TSettings> settingsSection, ISettingsWarningService warnings, IErrorNotifier notifier, ILogger logger, string taskId, string displayName, IReadOnlyCollection<string> warningIds); The base admission sequence is: Check cancellation and read the current typed settings. Skip when AutoUpdateEnabled is false. Skip when any configured warning is active. Call the optional ShouldRunInternalAsync predicate. Capture that settings snapshot in an admission calling ExecuteInternalAsync. Override these methods with the exact signatures: protected override Task<bool> ShouldRunInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { var view = args.CurrentActiveView; return Task.FromResult(view != null && (view.ViewType == ViewType.FloorPlan || view.ViewType == ViewType.CeilingPlan)); } protected override Task ExecuteInternalAsync( UIApplication uiapp, ViewActivatedEventArgs args, MyToolSettings settings, CancellationToken ct) { return _updater.UpdateAsync(uiapp, args.CurrentActiveView, settings, ct); } This excerpt assumes a tool-owned updater with that operation. Inject its real implementation. Filter cheap conditions before expensive work. Use shared transaction services for modifications and synchronous callbacks inside them. Do not create a transaction around asynchronous work. The base exposes Logger and a protected banner helper. It reads no settings again during execution, so the admitted values remain consistent and settings-read failures occur at admission. Dispatch and failure policy The hook resolves the document from args.CurrentActiveView and returns when there is no active document/view. It visits tasks in DI registration order. Each task is evaluated and executed through the safe executor. Outcome Result Null admission Skip the task for this event. Admission failure Record a document-session failure and activate the task's warning IDs. Execution failure Show the canonical auto-update failure banner and record a document-session failure. Do not automatically activate feature warnings. Cancellation Preserve the canceled outcome rather than classify it as a runtime failure. A runtime failure suppresses subsequent attempts for the task/document session. The gate uses DocumentSessionKey. Save As or the first save can create a new key, and reopening a document starts a new session. Clearing a feature warning alone does not erase the recorded runtime failure for that key. Tool prerequisite checks may explicitly activate an actionable warning and return without executing the update. Unexpected updater exceptions propagate. Feature Warnings owns the distinction between invalid configuration, admission failure, and execution failure. Core suppresses routine logs and presentation on the outer event dispatch. Admission uses error-only banners without start/completion logs. An admitted execution logs start/completion, suppresses generic executor banners, and uses one canonical runtime-failure banner. Keep detailed probes at Trace and log meaningful state changes. Do not suppress failure logs unless another published lifecycle owner observes and records that exact failure. IHookLifecycle Lifecycle hooks implement three operations: public interface IHookLifecycle { Task InitializeAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); Task RollbackAsync(UIControlledApplication application, CancellationToken ct); void Shutdown(UIControlledApplication application); } InitializeAsync acquires subscriptions and other owned state. If initialization fails partway, the implementation must undo its own partial work and preserve both initialization and cleanup failures. Record ownership immediately after subscription, before later logging or callbacks can fail. RollbackAsync reverses attachment when later startup work fails. It can queue into a valid Revit context because its continuation may run outside the original UI callback. Shutdown runs synchronously in Revit's shutdown callback. It must finish owned unsubscribe/removal work before returning. It has no cancellation token and cannot publish background work for later completion. Host ordering and rollback HookHost.AttachAsync resolves handlers, initializes lifecycle actions in registration order, then force-queues its ViewActivated subscription. It publishes attached state only after all actions succeed. The host records each attempted owner before initialization begins. Successfully initialized actions roll back in reverse order if attachment fails. The failing initializer owns its partial cleanup. Normal shutdown also reaches attempted owners whose initialization or rollback is incomplete. HookAttachAction cancels pending attachment, prevents later initialization or rollback dispatch after shutdown is requested, and makes completed shutdown idempotent. Cancellation failure does not prevent its shutdown callback. A failed callback remains available for retry. Late asynchronous attachment completion cannot invoke Revit shutdown callbacks from a background thread. HookLifecycleCoordinator attempts every reverse-order teardown action and aggregates contextual failures. Hooks and view tasks follow registration order. Group dependent operations in one hook or task when their ordering is part of the behavior. Contextual ribbon injectors DBTools.Core.Tools.Hooks.ContextualRibbon.ContextualRibbonInjector implements IHookLifecycle and IDisposable. Derive from it for tool-specific Edit buttons on contextual tabs. Super Girt Tool (SGT) supplies ContextualEditHook as an example. The derived type supplies tool/button/event names, the registered contextual command type, target tabs, selection evaluation, button construction, and edit flow. The base owns selection-change observation, injected controls, system-ID state, safe execution, and the edit ExternalEvent. Initialization queues API work to create the edit event, subscribe to selection changes, and evaluate the initial state. A partial failure immediately attempts unsubscribe, contextual UI removal, and edit-event disposal. Rollback uses the queued cleanup path. Normal shutdown uses synchronous cleanup and the exact detach action captured at successful subscription. Create ExternalEvent objects only in valid Revit API contexts. Autodesk ribbon command callbacks are not such a context. The base creates/refreshes its edit event through its managed Revit entry path. Contextual edit validates ContextualEditCommandType through CommandPreflight, sharing normal command registration and warning policy. Do not duplicate the base's event subscription or button registry in a derived type. FindTargetTabs, EvaluateSelection, BuildButton, and RunEditFlow are the tool-specific extension points. Synchronous shutdown Revit's IExternalApplication.OnShutdown is synchronous. AppShutdownLifecycle.Shutdown invokes AppShutdownWorkflow.RunSynchronously in that callback. It cancels startup, detaches hooks, and disposes runtime hosts before returning. It disposes the startup cancellation source only when startup is complete or absent. It neither queues Revit work nor pumps the dispatcher. Unfinished startup or deferred observation yields Result.Failed after owned teardown attempts. Core tracks WPF DispatcherOperation handles. Posting records ownership before BeginInvoke and rechecks retirement after the handle arrives. DispatcherOperationRegistry.Retire closes posting, releases callbacks and cancellation registrations, and aborts pending operations without executing their payloads. Their completion Tasks remain pending. Posts refused before queueing return canceled Tasks. WindowStaticRuntime.Reset does not retire that queue. Logger, ribbon, notification, and progress posts use WpfDispatcher.Post. Callback faults remain observable. A fault in an error reporter stays on the completion Task rather than escaping into Dispatcher.UnhandledException. Shutdown must not pump WPF or await retired dispatcher work. Extending and debugging hooks Use IHookLifecycle for another owned application subscription. Add an event-specific contract only when its dispatch shape requires one. Such a change must update the catalog, resolution, subscription, safe-execution policy, rollback, synchronous detach, and tests together. HookHost rejects an unknown contract. Registering it alone cannot attach an event. Symptom Check Lifecycle hook never initializes Register both its concrete DI service and RegisterHook<IHookLifecycle,T>() mapping. View task never runs Check its IViewActivationTask registration, settings, active warnings, predicate, and document-session failure gate. Startup rejects the task Check nonblank unique task IDs and known warning IDs. Handler resolution fails Register the concrete type and its constructor dependencies. UI freezes Remove synchronous waits and long work from UI callbacks. Re-enter the gate for API work after an await. Cleanup fails Inspect contextual errors for each unsubscribe, UI removal, and disposal attempt. Inspect %APPDATA%/DBTools/Logs/ first. Use the Settings Debug Mode control for runtime diagnostics rather than adding an unrelated logging configuration. See Testing Tools for fixture placement, compilation, and execution commands.

developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.title: Modularity | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/modularity.ht.summary: Modularity Tools use Core for execution, transactions, settings, logging, and window lifecycle. Presentation owns stable WPF shells, controls, resources, and themes. Tool assemblies own feature behavior, raw views, and ViewModels. Use constructor injection inside services. Resolve the first workflow from ICommandContext at the command boundary. Creating New Tools describes assembly ownership and module registration. Service lifetimes The application service root lasts for one runtime generation. A command or modeless session owns a run scope for Revit-dependent services. Service Lifetime Purpose ISafeExecutor Singleton Error policy, logging, and notifications at entrypoints. IAlertService Singleton Alert and selection dialogs. ISettingsProvider Singleton Fresh typed reads and atomic batch commits. ToolRegistry Application runtime Command and hook registrations. IRevitRunScope Scoped Current Revit application and document access. IRevitCallGate Scoped Synchronous API callbacks in a valid Revit context. ITransactionRunner Scoped Transactions for model changes. ITransactionGroupService Scoped Group health and commit/rollback. Use ILogger<T> through injection and context.Logger at command boundaries. The application logging host owns logger lifetime. Keep Document, UIDocument, and run-scope references within their command or session lifetime. Pass operation-specific document inputs or obtain verified current state from the run scope. Dispose the command/session scope only after its owned work and cleanup finish. Safe execution DBTools.Core.SafeExecution.Domain.ISafeExecutor defines two boundaries: Task RunAsync( Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IErrorNotifier? notifier, SafeExecutionOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<SafeExecutionResult> RunWithoutThrowingAsync( Func<Task> action, ILogger logger, IErrorNotifier? notifier, SafeExecutionOptions opts, CancellationToken ct = default); RunAsync propagates failures. RunWithoutThrowingAsync records an explicit outcome for a caller that must contain failure, such as a Revit event callback. Both provide correlation IDs, timing, cancellation admission, exception logging, and configured notifications. ToolCommand already owns this boundary. Let workflow failures reach it. SafeExecutionOptions requires an operation name: var options = new SafeExecutionOptions("Inspect Model") { BannerMode = SafeExecutionOptions.Mode.ErrorOnly }; await executor.RunAsync(InspectAsync, logger, notifier, options, ct); Option Default Effect LogStart true Log entry. LogCompletion true Log completion. LogFailure true Log a failed operation. BannerMode SuccessAndError Show success/error banners, errors only, or neither. FailureSurface Surface Surface fatal errors through the configured failure surface. CorrelationId Unspecified Supply an existing execution correlation ID. ErrorBanner(name, logStart, logCompletion) selects error-only banners. SuppressFailurePresentation(name) suppresses banners, fatal presentation, and routine start/completion logs while retaining failure logging. Disable LogFailure only when an already-published lifecycle owner observes and logs that same fault. Preserve the failed Task. App composition adapts the UI-owned log surface to ISafeExecutionFailureSurface. Window error boundaries use IWindowErrorLogSurface and WindowErrorPresenter. Consumers depend on these contracts rather than constructing concrete logger or notification windows. Use structured log fields: logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} elements in {Document}", count, document.Title); logger.LogError(exception, "Inspection failed for {Document}", document.Title); Use IAlertService for user decisions and IErrorNotifier for banners. Propagate failures through the safe-execution boundary with their context. Revit run scopes and call gates IRevitRunScope exposes UIApplication, CallGate, GetActiveUiDocument(), GetActiveDocument(), and GetVerifiedActiveDocument(expectedDocument, context). The verification method checks validity and DocumentSessionKey equality before returning the active document. Use the verification method before operating on a retained document. Run profile Gate Use InlineUi InlineRevitCallGate Commands already executing in a valid Revit API callback. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless work through the App-owned ExternalEvent host. The gate accepts synchronous callbacks: Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Await the returned Task outside the callback. Do not pass async lambdas into the gate. Async-state-machine Actions and known Task/ValueTask result shapes are rejected before execution. An awaitable hidden in object or an interface is rejected after the callback runs. Side effects remain. Custom awaiters are outside this check. A Revit API callback's context applies to its synchronous prefix. An async continuation must acquire a valid gate again before using the Revit API. InGate reports execution within a gate callback. It does not make arbitrary background work safe. On normal host retirement, pending queued work is dropped and its Tasks remain pending, even if cancellation arrives later. Shutdown must not await these Tasks. Failed-startup cleanup cancels pending work instead. See Revit execution for the full callback and shutdown contract. Transactions ITransactionRunner wraps synchronous model modifications: Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Use transaction.Document inside the callback: await transactions.RunInDocumentAsync(document, "DB Tools - Set Mark", transaction => { var element = transaction.Document.GetElement(elementId); element.LookupParameter("Mark").Set(mark); }, ct); The runner selects a SubTransaction when the document is modifiable and a new Transaction otherwise. It enforces document context and applies TransactionFailurePreprocessor. The callback rules match the call gate: no async Actions or Task/ValueTask results. Give each transaction a descriptive undo name. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService groups several transactions into one undo operation: bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); Finalize with TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit to assimilate the group or Rollback to discard it. IsGroupHealthyAsync returns true when no group exists and false when an active group has lost its healthy started state. The session/workflow owner must finalize on success, failure, and cancellation. Use a separate cancellation token for cleanup when the operation is canceled. Attempt all owned cleanup and retain both the operation and finalization errors. Do not use an unguarded finally exception that hides the operation's failure. Long-lived tool sessions also own the ordering of persistence, window closure, group finalization, and scope disposal. Alerts and selection IAlertService exposes request-based dialogs: AlertResult Show(AlertRequest request); bool Confirm(string message, IWindowOwnerHandleProvider ownerHandleProvider, string title = "DB Tools"); T? SelectSingle<T>(AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; IReadOnlyList<T> SelectMultiple<T>(AlertSelectionRequest<T> request) where T : class; Confirmation requires an owner provider. In a command: var alerts = context.Resolve<IAlertService>(); if (!alerts.Confirm("Delete the selected elements?", context.OwnerHandleProvider)) return; Selection requests supply choices, a display function, window title, header, and owned window options. For example: var selected = alerts.SelectSingle(new AlertSelectionRequest<Level>( levels, level => level.Name, "Select Level", "Target Level", new AlertWindowOptions(context.OwnerHandleProvider)) { Message = "Choose the target level." }); Core owns selection policy, body construction, and typed result extraction. Settings Inject ISettingsProvider and the typed SettingsSection<T>. Call Get(section) at the operation boundary for a fresh snapshot. Reads layer appsettings.json and the current per-year user file. Commit one or more section writes as a batch: var options = settings.Get(section); options.AutoUpdateEnabled = true; await settings.CommitAsync(new[] { section.CreateWrite(options) }, ct); Do not retain a settings snapshot in a singleton when subsequent operations need saved changes. Settings Packs owns DTO restrictions, source-generated metadata, file locking, save timing, and post-commit errors. Shared UI resources DBTools.Presentation.ThemeBrushKeys exposes ComponentResourceKey values. Use dynamic resources so the window's theme supplies each brush: <Border xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:theme="clr-namespace:DBTools.Presentation;assembly=DBTools.Presentation" Background="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Surface}}"> <TextBlock Text="Inspection" Foreground="{DynamicResource {x:Static theme:ThemeBrushKeys.Body}}" /> </Border> Keys cover brand, surface, text, status, and DataGrid brushes. Use the actual members in ThemeBrushKeys.cs and tokens in Resources/Tokens.xaml. Do not invent string keys or duplicate color values. Window-scoped resources avoid changing another add-in's theme. See the Theme System. Merge the stable Presentation theme into a raw view through ResourceUri: <Grid xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:resources="clr-namespace:DBTools.Presentation.Resources;assembly=DBTools.Presentation"> <Grid.Resources> <ResourceDictionary> <ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries> <ResourceDictionary Source="{resources:ResourceUri Resources/Theme.xaml}" /> </ResourceDictionary.MergedDictionaries> </ResourceDictionary> </Grid.Resources> </Grid> ResourceUri selects the loaded Presentation assembly's versioned resource URI. Keep raw views on stable resources rather than constructing payload pack URIs. Design tokens Resources/Tokens.xaml defines spacing, padding, corner radius, and typography. Use the token with the property type it expects: Token Type and value Spacing4, Spacing8, Spacing16 Thickness values of 4, 8, and 16. Spacing4.Value, Spacing8.Value, Spacing16.Value Double values for scalar properties. Pad8, Card.Padding Thickness values of 8 and 16,12. Radius4, Radius8 CornerRadius values of 4 and 8. FontSize.Body, FontSize.Title, FontSize.Header Double values of 13, 16, and 20. Tool-window sessions A raw tool view uses framework or stable Presentation types. It has no Window root, x:Class, code-behind event attributes, tool CLR namespaces, payload BAML, or implicit templates for tool types. Bind display values explicitly. Core's ToolWindowFactory installs the theme, owner, icon, error boundary, and progress lifecycle before parsing. It registers the session for normal closure and runtime-generation retirement: using var xaml = new MemoryStream(ToolWindowXaml.ReadEmbeddedResource( typeof(MyToolWindowViewModel).Assembly, "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml")); var session = factory.Create(ToolWindowKind.Modal, xaml, viewModel, new ToolWindowOptions { Title = "My Tool", Width = 800, Height = 600 }); _ = session.ShowDialog(); Use ToolWindowKind.Modeless and session.Show() for a modeless surface. Register payload handlers and owned cleanup through the session. A custom initializeShell callback owns the initializer it creates and must register its disposal through session.AddCleanup. Normal close dispatches payload Closed handlers before releasing owned state. Retirement of an open session also clears its view graph. Keep the application run scope alive through failure-bearing session completion. Window.Close() alone does not establish that asynchronous cleanup finished. Presentation owns shells and ToolWindowCallbackScope. Core and tool assemblies can belong to a replaceable product generation. Stable controls and resources must not retain a retired ViewModel, callback, or tool type. This contract also applies to Settings, alerts, logger windows, banners, and progress UI. Sandbox Integration covers previews and native WPF validation. Hooks covers subscriptions that also need generation-safe shutdown.

developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.title: Creating New Tools | DB Tools
developer-guide/developing/new-tool-guid.summary: Creating New Tools A DB Tools tool owns its source, manifest, resources, production assembly, and tests. App discovers embedded manifests, registers services, and composes ribbon controls. Each tool assembly ships under the product year's Tools/ directory. Service and settings modules follow the same assembly contract as ribbon tools. Use this page to create the tool boundary. See Modularity for runtime services, Settings Packs for configuration, Hooks for events, and Testing Tools for validation. Prerequisites Run commands from the repository root. Desktop builds support Revit 2026 (2026.5 or later) and Revit 2027. Both use net10.0-windows. The selected year chooses API references and output directories. APS Design Automation uses a separate Revit 2026/.NET 8 contract. Check the build entrypoint before adding a tool: ./build.sh --help ./build.sh BuildApp -y 2026 On native Windows, use the PowerShell entrypoint: pwsh -NoProfile -File build.ps1 BuildApp -y 2026 build.sh supports Linux and WSL. It refuses native Windows shells. The wrappers acquire the SDK pinned in global.json and initialize the HandyControl submodule when needed. Build and validation commands explains the targets, defaults, logs, and source gates. 1. Choose the owner and names Place a tool under src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/. Categories such as Common, Structural, Experimental, and Services organize source. They do not enter CLR namespaces. A tool's namespace root is DBTools.<Tool>. Follow the repository's .agents/canon/CANON.md naming contract: Mirror folders in namespaces beneath the component root. Give each C# identity its own file with the same name. Partial companions may use dotted suffixes, such as Workflow.Validation.cs. Put manifest-facing commands and modules under App/Composition/. Put whole-tool composition, windows, navigation, and session lifetime under App/. Put user capabilities under Features/<Concept>/ and shared tool language under Domain/. Put Revit adapters beneath the nearest owning concept's Revit/ folder. Create only populated owners. CANON bans Shell and Shared as production owners and treats Models as a generic kind bucket. For example: src/Tools/Common/MyTool/ ├── App/ │ ├── Composition/ │ │ ├── MyToolCommand.cs │ │ └── MyToolToolModule.cs │ ├── DesignTime/ │ │ └── MyToolWindowDesignTimeViewModel.cs │ ├── ViewModels/ │ │ └── MyToolWindowViewModel.cs │ └── Views/ │ └── MyToolWindow.xaml ├── Assets/ │ └── my_tool.png ├── Features/ │ └── Inspection/ │ └── InspectionWorkflow.cs ├── Settings/ ├── Tests/ ├── DBTools.MyTool.csproj └── manifest.yml The optional Settings/ and Tests/ entries represent actual content, not placeholder directories. Short tool prefixes use Pascal-compressed forms such as Gm, Sgt, and Tdv. Window names pair with their runtime and design-time ViewModels, for example GmWindow, GmWindowViewModel, and GmWindowDesignTimeViewModel. 2. Create the production project Every tool manifest root needs a production project with DBT_IsToolAssembly=true, including a module with no ribbon commands. Add production and test projects to DBTools.sln under the owning solution folder. This project is a starting point for the example tool's DBTools.MyTool.csproj: <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"> <PropertyGroup> <TargetFramework>$(DBT_RevitTargetFramework)</TargetFramework> <DBT_RevitHostIdentity>$(DBT_DesktopRevitHostIdentity)</DBT_RevitHostIdentity> <DBT_IsToolAssembly>true</DBT_IsToolAssembly> <RootNamespace>DBTools.MyTool</RootNamespace> <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion> <Nullable>enable</Nullable> <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <Compile Remove="Tests\**\*.cs" /> <ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\DBTools.Core\DBTools.Core.csproj" /> <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions" /> <EmbeddedResource Include="Assets\*.png"> <Link>Resources\Icons\%(Filename)%(Extension)</Link> </EmbeddedResource> </ItemGroup> </Project> The repository supplies year-specific Revit API metadata packages through Directory.Build.targets. Do not copy installed Revit DLLs into the product. Declare a direct, versionless package reference when source uses that package's API. Prefer the smallest package that supplies the API. When tests need internal production types, declare visibility in the tool project for the exact consuming assembly names: <ItemGroup> <InternalsVisibleTo Include="DBTools.MyTool.Pure.Tests" /> <InternalsVisibleTo Include="DBTools.MyTool.Local.Tests" /> </ItemGroup> Content-derived assembly identity applies by default to tool assemblies through build/MSBuild/ContentVersion.targets. This includes non-WPF tools. For WPF, add UseWPF=true, reference Presentation where used, and add CommunityToolkit.Mvvm when using its generators. Tool views are raw embedded XAML. Disable automatic Page compilation and give each raw resource an explicit logical name: <PropertyGroup> <UseWPF>true</UseWPF> <EnableDefaultPageItems>false</EnableDefaultPageItems> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\DBTools.Presentation\DBTools.Presentation.csproj" /> <PackageReference Include="CommunityToolkit.Mvvm" /> <EmbeddedResource Include="App\Views\MyToolWindow.xaml" LogicalName="DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolWindow.xaml" /> </ItemGroup> Tools with Revit-dependent designer source can exclude **\Revit\**\*.cs when DesignTimeBuild=true. Keep designer-only resource dictionaries separate from runtime raw views. If a project compiles Properties\DesignTimeResources.xaml, its Page metadata can declare SubType=Designer, Generator=MSBuild:Compile, and ContainsDesignTimeResources=true. 3. Declare the manifest A ribbon module can use this manifest: id: DBTools.MyTool assembly: DBTools.MyTool moduleType: DBTools.MyTool.App.Composition.MyToolToolModule order: 0 panel: Common tool: ribbonTools: - internalName: DBTools.MyTool commandType: DBTools.MyTool.App.Composition.MyToolCommand availabilityType: DBTools.MyTool.App.Composition.MyToolCommand runProfile: InlineUi displayText: "My Tool" iconBaseKey: my_tool tooltip: "Inspect the active model" controlKind: PushButton order: 50 assembly is the actual simple assembly name without .dll. App embeds manifests centrally, but compiles no tool source, XAML, or assets. The product build discovers declared tool projects and stages their assemblies under <year>/Tools/. build/MSBuild/ProductOutput.proj builds and stages those owners. ToolAssemblyResolver loads the declared file in the root assembly's owning context. Runtime resolves modules, commands, icons, and raw views from that owner. Manifest fields Field Requirement and meaning id Required unique tool identifier. assembly Required simple assembly name. moduleType Optional fully qualified ToolModule type. order Required load order, lower first. Use 0 without an ordering requirement. panel Required for every ribbon manifest and by settings-pack registration. Accepted values: Settings, Common, Structural, Testing, Services. tool.settings.configSection Optional single JSON property name in settings.<year>.json. tool.settingsPacks Optional pack definitions with required key and title. tool.ribbonTools Ribbon command definitions. May be absent for a service/settings/hook module. sandboxWindows Optional raw-view previews. See Sandbox Integration. A module must own at least one responsibility: ribbon tools, settings, settings packs, or registered hooks. A moduleless manifest requires panel and at least one ribbon tool. It cannot declare settings or settings packs. For a service module, retain the project and declare its actual owner: id: DBTools.DialogSuppression assembly: DBTools.DialogSuppression moduleType: DBTools.DialogSuppression.App.Composition.DialogSuppressionToolModule order: -1 panel: Services tool: settings: configSection: Tools.DialogSuppression settingsPacks: - key: services.dialog_suppression title: "Dialog Suppression" Ribbon fields Field Requirement and meaning internalName Required unique control identity, also used by warning definitions. commandType Required fully qualified concrete ToolCommand type. availabilityType Optional concrete command type implementing IExternalCommandAvailability. runProfile InlineUi by default, or QueuedModeless. displayText Required label. YAML double-quoted strings support \n line breaks. iconBaseKey Required embedded icon key without extension. tooltip Required tooltip text. controlKind PushButton by default, or SplitButtonItem, PulldownButtonItem, StackedButtonItem. splitGroup Required nonblank group for grouped controls. Invalid for a push button. order Required order within the panel/group. groupDisplayText Optional group header text. groupTooltip Optional group header tooltip. groupIconBaseKey Optional group header icon key. Optional values cannot be blank. Push buttons cannot carry grouped-control metadata. Entries sharing a split or pulldown group form one ordered sequence. The lowest-order split entry is the primary command. The remaining entries are its dropdown commands. App planning and Revit construction use that sequence. Use a 32×32 main icon such as my_tool.png. An optional 16×16 companion is my_tool_16.png. Match the base filename to iconBaseKey. 4. Register services ToolModule lives in DBTools.Core.Tools.Modules.Composition. Its registration methods receive the manifest from DBTools.Core.Tools.Manifest: Method Contribution RegisterSettings Typed persistence sections. RegisterServices Tool services and dependency injection registrations. RegisterSettingsPacks Settings catalog definitions and context/view factories. RegisterHooks Hook implementation mappings in ToolRegistry. Startup calls RegisterSettings, RegisterServices, RegisterSettingsPacks, and RegisterHooks in that order for each module before validating and merging its registrations. Keep modules limited to composition. Put behavior with the feature that owns it. For example, a module can register a feature workflow: using DBTools.Core.Tools.Manifest; using DBTools.Core.Tools.Modules.Composition; using DBTools.MyTool.Features.Inspection; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; namespace DBTools.MyTool.App.Composition; public sealed class MyToolToolModule : ToolModule { public override void RegisterServices(IServiceCollection services, ToolManifest manifest) { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(services); ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(manifest); services.AddScoped<InspectionWorkflow>(); } } A simple moduleless command may declare [CommandService(typeof(Workflow))] on the command. Framing Joins uses this pattern for FramingJoinsWorkflow. Do not reconstruct ribbon registrations in a module. App resolves concrete command and availability types. Core constructs their shared registrations. 5. Implement the command Use ToolCommand from DBTools.Core.Tools.Commands for ribbon commands. It supplies safe execution, contextual logging, command preflight, and scope creation/disposal. Revit constructs the command with an inert parameterless constructor.
